AFG.a: A landlocked, mountainous country between Central and South Asia, at the crossroads of old routes between Persia, India and the steppes. Ahmad Shah Durrani founded it in 1747, and in the 19th century it was a buffer between the British and Russian empires, fully independent from 1919. A coup in 1973 and a communist one in 1978 led to the Soviet invasion of 1979 and a decade of war, then civil war and the rise of the Taliban in the 1990s. After the attacks of 11 September 2001 a US-led intervention removed the Taliban, who returned to power in 2021 as foreign forces withdrew. Pashto and Dari are its main languages, and farming and herding still support many of its people. The empty niches of Bamiyan, where giant Buddhas stood until 2001, and the blue-tiled shrine of Mazar-i-Sharif recall its long history.
AFG.f: The Hindu Kush divides the country, and its highest peaks rise in the Wakhan Corridor, a narrow strip that reaches China.

AGO.a: A large country on Africa's south-west coast, whose north was part of the Kingdom of Kongo before the Portuguese founded Luanda in 1576 and made it a hub of the Atlantic slave trade. It won independence in 1975 after a long war against Portuguese rule, then suffered a civil war that lasted, with pauses, until 2002. Oil and diamonds have made it one of Africa's largest economies. Its land runs from rainforest in the north to the edge of the Namib Desert in the south, with the Kalandula Falls on the Lucala River among its sights. Portuguese is its official language, spoken alongside Umbundu, Kimbundu and Kikongo.
AGO.f: Its province of Cabinda is cut off from the rest of the country by a strip of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

ALB.a: A small, mountainous country on the Adriatic and Ionian coasts of the Balkans. Illyrians, Greeks and Romans left their mark here, and in the 15th century Skanderbeg held off the Ottomans for a quarter of a century before the country fell under their rule until independence in 1912. After the Second World War it lived under one of Europe's most isolated communist regimes, which ended in the early 1990s. Today it is a candidate to join the European Union, and its beaches and mountains draw ever more visitors. Its language, Albanian, forms a branch of its own in the Indo-European family.
ALB.f: Under communist rule it built some 170,000 concrete bunkers against an invasion that never came.

AND.a: A tiny principality high in the Pyrenees between France and Spain, the last survivor of the border states that Charlemagne set up against the Moors. A pact of 1278 set up the joint rule that still shapes it, and it adopted its first written constitution only in 1993. Today it lives mostly from tourism, skiing and shoppers drawn by its low taxes. Catalan is its official language.
AND.f: It has two heads of state at once: the President of France and the Bishop of Urgell in Spain.

ARE.a: A federation of seven emirates on the Persian Gulf, formed in 1971 when the Trucial States left British protection; Ras al-Khaimah joined in 1972. Pearling and trade sustained the coast until oil was found in the late 1950s and transformed it within a generation. Abu Dhabi, the largest emirate, holds most of the oil, while Dubai has become a world hub for trade, flights and tourism. Most of the people living here are foreign workers, above all from South Asia. Inland lie the dunes of the Empty Quarter and the oasis city of Al Ain.
ARE.f: Dubai's Burj Khalifa, 828 m tall, has been the tallest building in the world since 2010.

ARG.a: The second-largest country in South America, reaching from the subtropical north to Tierra del Fuego, independent from Spain since 1816. Its heartland is the Pampas, the vast grassland whose cattle and wheat made it one of the richest countries in the world around 1900. Waves of immigrants, above all from Italy and Spain, shaped its cities, and Buenos Aires is the city of tango. The 20th century brought Peronism, military coups and a "Dirty War" that ended with democracy in 1983, a year after its defeat in the war with Britain over the Falkland Islands (Malvinas). Its landscapes range from the Iguazú Falls in the north-east to the glaciers of Patagonia, the Perito Moreno among them. Football, asado and mate are national passions.
ARG.f: Aconcagua is the highest mountain outside Asia, and the highest in both the Western and the Southern Hemisphere.

ARM.a: A landlocked country in the mountains of the South Caucasus, with a language, an alphabet and a church of its own. Its kingdom was briefly a great power under Tigranes the Great in the 1st century BC, and its alphabet was devised around 405 by the monk Mesrop Mashtots. Over the centuries it was ruled by Persians, Byzantines, Arabs, Mongols, Ottomans and Russians. During the First World War the Armenians of the Ottoman Empire suffered deportations and massacres in which around a million people died, the Armenian Genocide. It became independent from the Soviet Union in 1991. Mount Ararat, a national symbol, rises in sight of the capital, Yerevan, but stands across the border in Türkiye, and monasteries such as Geghard and Tatev cling to its gorges.
ARM.f: It was the first state to adopt Christianity, early in the 4th century.

ATG.a: Two main islands and many small ones in the Leeward Islands of the Caribbean, a British colony until 1981. Sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans once covered Antigua, and English Harbour was a base of the Royal Navy, where Nelson's Dockyard still stands. Today tourism drives its economy, and Antigua Sailing Week is among the great regattas of the Caribbean. Barbuda, flat and quiet, is known for its pink-sand beaches and a large colony of frigatebirds.
ATG.f: Antigua is said to have 365 beaches, one for every day of the year.

AUS.a: The world's sixth-largest country and its smallest continent, home to people for at least 50,000 years. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples hold some of the oldest living cultures on Earth, whose rock art and songlines cross the land. Britain founded a penal colony at Sydney in 1788, and six colonies joined as the Commonwealth of Australia in 1901. Most Australians live in cities along the coasts, Sydney and Melbourne the largest, while the dry interior, the outback, is among the emptiest land on Earth. Uluru rises from its red centre, and the Great Barrier Reef, the largest coral reef system in the world, runs along the Queensland coast. Koalas, wombats and platypuses are among the animals found nowhere else. Its economy rests on services, mining and farming.
AUS.f: It is the largest country in the world without a land border.

AUT.a: A landlocked country in Central Europe, about two-thirds of it in the Alps. The Habsburgs, who ruled from Vienna for more than six centuries, built an empire across Central Europe, and for a time their family also held Spain and its empire. After the First World War it became a small republic; Nazi Germany annexed it in 1938, and it regained full independence in 1955 on the condition of permanent neutrality. Vienna was the city of Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven and Schubert, of Freud and the coffee house, and still holds a season of balls every winter. Salzburg, Mozart's birthplace, the lakes of the Salzkammergut and the peaks of the Tyrol draw visitors in every season. It joined the European Union in 1995.
AUT.f: Vienna's Schönbrunn Zoo, opened in 1752, is the oldest zoo in the world still open.

AZE.a: A country between the Caucasus Mountains and the Caspian Sea, where Europe meets Asia. Persian, Arab, Turkic and Russian rule all shaped it before a short-lived republic in 1918, one of the first in the Muslim world, and seven decades in the Soviet Union until independence in 1991. Oil has been drawn here since ancient times; around 1900 Baku produced about half of the world's oil, and oil and gas still drive its economy. The walled old city of Baku holds the Maiden Tower and the Palace of the Shirvanshahs. Fires that burn on gas seeping from the ground, as at Yanar Dag, gave it the name "land of fire".
AZE.f: Its long coast is on the Caspian Sea, which is a lake, so the country is landlocked.

BDI.a: A small, landlocked country of hills in the Great Lakes region of Africa, on the north-east shore of Lake Tanganyika. A kingdom for centuries, it came under German and then Belgian rule, and became independent in 1962. Conflict between Hutu and Tutsi marked much of its history, including a civil war from 1993 to 2005. Most of its people farm, coffee and tea are among its main exports, and its royal drummers, whose ritual UNESCO lists, are famous far beyond its borders.
BDI.f: It lies on the divide between the basins of the Nile and the Congo.

BEL.a: A small country on the North Sea, between France, Germany, Luxembourg and the Netherlands. It is divided between Dutch-speaking Flanders in the north and French-speaking Wallonia in the south, with bilingual Brussels and a small German-speaking community in the east. Its cities, Bruges, Ghent and Antwerp, grew rich on cloth and trade in the Middle Ages and gave Europe the Flemish painters, from Van Eyck to Rubens. It became independent from the Netherlands in 1830 and was the first country on the continent to industrialise. Fought over in both world wars, it was a founder of what became the European Union, and Brussels hosts the Union's main institutions and NATO's headquarters. Its chocolate, waffles, fries and hundreds of beers are famous far beyond its borders.
BEL.f: Tintin, the Smurfs and the saxophone were all invented by Belgians.

BEN.a: A narrow country in West Africa, stretching some 650 km from the Bight of Benin to the Niger River. In the south rose the Kingdom of Dahomey, remembered for its royal palaces at Abomey and its women soldiers, the Agojie, and enriched in part by the Atlantic slave trade. A French colony, it became independent in 1960, and in 1990 and 1991 it was among the first African countries to move peacefully from one-party rule to democracy. Ganvié, a town on stilts in Lake Nokoué, and the national parks of the north, home to lions and elephants, are among its sights.
BEN.f: Vodun, the religion known abroad as voodoo, began here, and a national holiday honours it every 10 January.

BFA.a: A landlocked country in the Sahel of West Africa, formerly Upper Volta, a French colony until 1960. The Mossi kingdoms, founded centuries ago, still have their kings, the Mogho Naaba among them in Ouagadougou. It took its present name in 1984, under Thomas Sankara. Most of its people farm, and cotton and gold are its main exports. Ouagadougou hosts FESPACO, the largest film festival in Africa, every two years.
BFA.f: Its name means 'land of upright people', joining words from two of its languages, Mooré and Dyula.

BGD.a: A low, fertile country on the delta of the Ganges, the Brahmaputra and the Meghna, among the most densely populated on Earth. Part of Bengal, it became the eastern part of Pakistan when British India was divided in 1947, and won independence in 1971 after a war of liberation. Its rivers bring both rich soil and floods, and cyclones from the Bay of Bengal strike its coast. It has grown fast on its garment industry, one of the largest in the world. Bengali, whose defence in 1952 is remembered every 21 February, is spoken by nearly everyone, and Cox's Bazar has one of the longest natural beaches in the world.
BGD.f: It shares the Sundarbans, the largest mangrove forest in the world, with India.

BGR.a: A country in the east of the Balkans, between the Danube and the Black Sea, with the Balkan and Rila mountains at its heart. The Thracians lived here before the Bulgars founded a state in 681, which grew into one of the great powers of medieval Europe. After nearly five centuries of Ottoman rule it became an autonomous principality in 1878 and fully independent in 1908, and after the Second World War it was a communist state until 1989. It joined NATO in 2004 and the European Union in 2007. The Rila Monastery, its Thracian tombs and the Valley of Roses, whose flowers are grown for their oil, are among its treasures.
BGR.f: The Cyrillic alphabet took shape here, in the First Bulgarian Empire, in the 9th and 10th centuries.

BHR.a: An archipelago in the Persian Gulf, the smallest country in the Middle East. As Dilmun it was a trading hub between Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley more than 4,000 years ago, and later it was famous for its pearls. In 1932 it became the first place on the Arab side of the Gulf to strike oil, and it has since grown into a centre of banking. A British protectorate, it became independent in 1971.
BHR.f: The King Fahd Causeway, about 25 km of bridges and embankments, links it to Saudi Arabia.

BHS.a: Some 700 islands and thousands of cays on the edge of the Atlantic, south-east of Florida, about 30 of them inhabited. Columbus made his first landfall in the Americas here in 1492, probably on San Salvador. The islands were a haunt of pirates in the early 18th century and a British colony until independence in 1973. Today tourism and banking are its mainstays, and the turquoise shallows of its banks surround islands such as Andros, Eleuthera and the Exumas.
BHS.f: On Big Major Cay, in the Exumas, wild pigs swim out to meet the boats.

BIH.a: A mountainous country in the western Balkans, home to Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats, where mosques, Orthodox and Catholic churches and synagogues stand close together in Sarajevo. A medieval kingdom, it was ruled by the Ottomans from the 15th century and by Austria-Hungary from 1878; in Sarajevo in 1914 the murder of Archduke Franz Ferdinand set off the First World War. Part of Yugoslavia after both world wars, it declared independence in 1992, which was followed by war until 1995, including the Srebrenica genocide. The Dayton Agreement that ended it divided the country into two entities. The old bridge of Mostar, destroyed in 1993 and rebuilt in 2004, has become a symbol of the country.
BIH.f: Its whole coast, at Neum, is only about 20 km long, and splits Croatia's coast in two.

BLR.a: A landlocked country of plains, forests and marshes in Eastern Europe, between Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, Russia and Ukraine. For centuries its lands belonged to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, before passing to the Russian Empire in the late 18th century. It suffered terribly in the Second World War, losing about a quarter of its people, and was a Soviet republic until independence in 1991. More than a third of it is forest, and the Polesia marshes in the south are among the largest wetlands in Europe. The castles of Mir and Nesvizh are listed by UNESCO.
BLR.f: Białowieża Forest, on its border with Poland, is a last piece of Europe's ancient forest, where wild bison still roam.

BLZ.a: A small country on the Caribbean coast of Central America, once British Honduras, independent since 1981 and the only country in Central America with English as its official language. Maya cities such as Caracol and Lamanai lie in its forests, which also shelter jaguars in the world's first jaguar reserve, the Cockscomb Basin. Its people include Mestizo, Creole, Maya and Garifuna communities, and Mennonite farmers. Offshore lie hundreds of small islands, the cays, loved by divers.
BLZ.f: Its barrier reef, home to the Great Blue Hole, is the largest in the Western Hemisphere.

BOL.a: A landlocked country in the heart of South America, reaching from the high Altiplano of the Andes down to the Amazon rainforest and the Chaco. Tiwanaku, near Lake Titicaca, was the centre of a great Andean civilisation, and the Inca empire later ruled the highlands. Under Spain the silver of Potosí's Cerro Rico made the city one of the largest in the Americas. It became independent in 1825, took its name from Simón Bolívar, and lost its coast to Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879 to 1884). Many of its people are Indigenous, Quechua and Aymara above all. Sucre is its constitutional capital, while the government sits in La Paz, the highest seat of government in the world, and the Salar de Uyuni is the largest salt flat on Earth.
BOL.f: It shares Lake Titicaca, the highest navigable lake in the world, with Peru.

BRA.a: The largest country in South America, covering nearly half of the continent, and the only one where Portuguese is the main language. Portugal claimed it in 1500 and built a colony of sugar, then gold and coffee, worked by millions of enslaved Africans, more than anywhere else in the Americas. It became independent in 1822 as an empire under a Portuguese prince, abolished slavery in 1888, the last country in the Americas to do so, and became a republic in 1889. The Amazon rainforest, the largest on Earth, covers much of the north. Its people descend from Indigenous peoples, Europeans and Africans, and from later Japanese and Middle Eastern immigrants. Rio de Janeiro's carnival, samba, bossa nova and its football are known all over the world. São Paulo is the largest city in the Southern Hemisphere, and Brasília, its modernist capital, was built from nothing in the late 1950s. It is one of the world's great farming powers, for soy, coffee, sugar and beef.
BRA.f: It borders every other South American country except Chile and Ecuador.

BRB.a: A small coral island in the West Indies, English and then British from 1627 until independence in 1966. Sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans made it one of England's richest colonies in the 17th century. It became a republic in 2021, and lives from tourism and finance. Cricket is a passion, and the Crop Over festival celebrates the end of the sugar harvest.
BRB.f: It is the easternmost island of the Caribbean.

BRN.a: A small sultanate on the north coast of Borneo, whose sultans once ruled much of the island's coast and parts of the Philippines. A British protectorate from 1888, it became fully independent in 1984. Oil and gas, found in 1929, made it one of the richest countries in Asia. Rainforest covers most of its land, and Kampong Ayer, a village of houses on stilts in the river at Bandar Seri Begawan, has stood for centuries.
BRN.f: It is in two parts, separated by Malaysia; the eastern one, Temburong, is almost surrounded by it.

BTN.a: A small Buddhist kingdom in the eastern Himalayas, between China and India, rising from subtropical forest to glaciers above 7,000 m. Unified in the 17th century by Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal, it has been ruled by the Wangchuck kings since 1907 and became a constitutional monarchy in 2008. It measures its progress by Gross National Happiness, keeps most of its land under forest, and asks visitors to pay a daily fee. Its fortress-monasteries, the dzongs, and the Tiger's Nest monastery on a cliff above Paro are among the sights of the Himalayas.
BTN.f: Its highest mountain, Gangkhar Puensum, is the highest in the world that has never been climbed.

BWA.a: A landlocked country in southern Africa, most of it covered by the Kalahari. As the British protectorate of Bechuanaland it was one of the poorest places in the world when it became independent in 1966; diamonds found soon after, and careful government, made it one of Africa's success stories. It has been a stable democracy ever since. Its wildlife is among the richest in Africa, with the largest population of elephants on the continent, in Chobe and around the Okavango. English is its official language, and Setswana is spoken by most of its people.
BWA.f: The Okavango is a great river delta that never reaches the sea; its waters fade into the Kalahari.

CAF.a: A landlocked country of savanna and forest in Central Africa, between the Sahel and the Congo basin. Once Ubangi-Shari, part of French Equatorial Africa, it became independent in 1960, and has since known coups, an emperor who crowned himself, Bokassa, in the 1970s, and long periods of conflict. Its forests at Dzanga-Sangha are home to forest elephants and western lowland gorillas, and its rivers drain to the Congo and to Lake Chad. Sango, spoken by nearly everyone, is an official language alongside French.
CAF.f: It lies almost exactly at the centre of the African continent.

CAN.a: The second-largest country in the world, reaching from the Atlantic to the Pacific and north into the Arctic. First Nations and Inuit lived here long before French and British colonists, whose rivalry ended with British rule in 1763; the Métis were born of their meeting. Confederation in 1867 joined the first provinces into a dominion, which grew to ten provinces and three territories and became fully sovereign step by step until 1982. English and French are both official, and Québec keeps its French language and culture. Most Canadians live within a few hundred kilometres of the US border, in cities such as Toronto, Montréal and Vancouver, while the north is a land of forest, tundra and countless lakes. The Rocky Mountains of Banff and Jasper, Niagara Falls and the Bay of Fundy, with the highest tides in the world, are among its wonders.
CAN.f: It has the longest coastline of any country in the world.

CHE.a: A small, mountainous country in the heart of Europe, where the Alps cover about 60% of the land and the Jura and a central plateau share the rest. It grew from an alliance of three cantons in 1291 into a confederation of 26 cantons, with direct democracy: its citizens vote on laws and changes to the constitution several times a year. It has four national languages, German, French, Italian and Romansh. Geneva hosts many international organisations, among them the Red Cross, founded there in 1863, and the United Nations' European headquarters. Banking, watches, chocolate, cheese and precision industry made it one of the richest countries in the world. The Matterhorn, the Jungfrau and lakes such as Geneva and Lucerne draw visitors all year.
CHE.f: It has stayed neutral in international wars since 1815.

CHL.a: A long, narrow country between the Andes and the Pacific, from the Atacama, the driest non-polar desert on Earth, to the glaciers and fjords of Patagonia and Cape Horn. The Inca ruled its north, while in the south the Mapuche long resisted first the Inca and then Spain. It became independent in 1818, and won the nitrate and copper lands of the north in the War of the Pacific. In 1973 a military coup brought General Pinochet to power until 1990, when democracy returned. It is the world's largest producer of copper, and its central valleys grow wine and fruit. Easter Island, with its giant moai statues, lies some 3,500 km out in the Pacific.
CHL.f: It is some 4,300 km long, yet on average only about 175 km wide.

CHN.a: The most populous country in the world for centuries, until India passed it in 2023, and the third or fourth largest by area. Its civilisation grew along the Yellow and Yangtze rivers over more than 3,000 years of written history, ruled by dynasties from the Shang to the Qing. Paper, printing, the compass and gunpowder were invented here, and the Great Wall and the Silk Road recall its empires. The last emperor fell in 1912, and after decades of war the Communist Party founded the People's Republic in 1949. Since reforms began in 1978 it has grown into the world's second-largest economy and its largest manufacturer. Its landscapes range from the Tibetan Plateau and the Himalayas to the Gobi Desert and the karst peaks of Guilin. Mandarin is its official language, and most of its people are Han Chinese, alongside 55 recognised minorities.
CHN.f: The whole country, nearly 5,000 km wide, keeps a single time zone.

CIV.a: A country on the Gulf of Guinea in West Africa, with lagoons along its coast, rainforest in the south and savanna in the north. A French colony, it became independent in 1960, and under its first president, Félix Houphouët-Boigny, it grew into one of the most prosperous countries in the region. Conflicts from 2002 to 2011 interrupted that growth, which has since resumed. Abidjan is its largest city and economic heart, while Yamoussoukro, the official capital, holds the Basilica of Our Lady of Peace, among the largest churches in the world. It has some 60 ethnic groups, and French is its official language.
CIV.f: It is the largest producer of cocoa beans in the world.

CMR.a: A country where West and Central Africa meet, between the Gulf of Guinea and Lake Chad. A German colony from 1884, it was divided between France and Britain after the First World War; the French part became independent in 1960, and part of the British south joined it in 1961. That is why it has two official languages, French and English, alongside some 250 local ones. Mount Cameroon, an active volcano, rises from the coast. Its football team, the Indomitable Lions, was the first from Africa to reach a World Cup quarter-final, in 1990.
CMR.f: It is called 'Africa in miniature' for holding nearly every landscape of the continent.

COD.a: The second-largest country in Africa, most of it in the basin of the Congo River and covered by the second-largest rainforest on Earth. The Kingdom of Kongo, the Luba and the Lunda once ruled parts of it. From 1885 it was the personal property of King Leopold II of Belgium, whose regime of forced labour for rubber killed and maimed vast numbers of people, until Belgium took it over as a colony in 1908. Independent since 1960, it was known as Zaire from 1971 to 1997, and wars from 1996 to 2003, drawing in its neighbours, cost millions of lives. Its ground holds immense wealth in copper, cobalt, diamonds and gold, and it produces most of the world's cobalt. Kinshasa is among the largest French-speaking cities in the world, and the rumba of the two Congos is listed by UNESCO. Its forests shelter okapis, bonobos and mountain gorillas.
COD.f: The Congo is the deepest river in the world, more than 200 m deep in places.

COG.a: A country of rainforest and savanna astride the equator, on the right bank of the Congo and Ubangi rivers. Part of the Kingdom of Loango and other states before France claimed it in the 1880s, it became the heart of French Equatorial Africa, and Brazzaville served as the capital of Free France during the Second World War. Independent since 1960, it has lived through Marxist rule and civil wars in the 1990s. Oil from offshore fields drives its economy, and its forests, as in Odzala-Kokoua and Nouabalé-Ndoki, shelter gorillas and forest elephants.
COG.f: Brazzaville faces Kinshasa across the Congo River, the closest pair of capitals in the world after Rome and the Vatican.

COL.a: A country in the north-west of South America, where three ranges of the Andes fan out between the Amazon, the plains of the Orinoco and the sea. Spain founded Santa Marta and Cartagena in the 16th century, and Simón Bolívar won its independence in 1819, as part of Gran Colombia. It is one of the most biodiverse countries on Earth, with more species of birds than any other country. A long conflict between the state, guerrillas, paramilitaries and drug cartels marked the late 20th century, and a peace deal with the largest guerrilla group, the FARC, was signed in 2016. Its coffee is famous worldwide, it is the leading source of emeralds, and Gabriel García Márquez made its towns the setting of magical realism. Cartagena's walled old town, Medellín and Bogotá, high in the Andes, draw ever more visitors.
COL.f: It is the only South American country with coasts on both the Pacific and the Caribbean.

COM.a: Three volcanic islands, Grande Comore, Mohéli and Anjouan, at the northern mouth of the Mozambique Channel, between Mozambique and Madagascar. Arab, African and Malagasy influences mixed here over centuries of trade, and its sultanates came under French rule in the 19th century. It declared independence in 1975, but the fourth island, Mayotte, chose to stay French, and the country has known many coups since. Mount Karthala, a large active volcano, rises on Grande Comore, and the islands grow much of the world's ylang-ylang, used in perfume.
COM.f: It is the only country of the Arab League that lies wholly in the Southern Hemisphere.

CPV.a: Ten volcanic islands in the Atlantic, about 570 km off the coast of Senegal, uninhabited until the Portuguese settled them in the 15th century. They became a hub of the Atlantic slave trade and a stop for ships crossing the ocean. Independent from Portugal since 1975, it has become one of Africa's most stable democracies. More of its people live abroad than at home, and its music, morna, sung by Cesária Évora, is listed by UNESCO. Portuguese is its official language, alongside the Cape Verdean Creole that everyone speaks.
CPV.f: Its active volcano, Pico do Fogo, last erupted in 2014 and 2015.

CRI.a: A small country between the Caribbean and the Pacific in Central America, with a spine of volcanoes, cloud forests and beaches on both coasts. A Spanish colony, it became independent in 1821 and grew rich on coffee and then bananas. Since a short civil war in 1948 it has been one of the most stable democracies in Latin America. About a quarter of its land is protected, and it holds some 5% of the world's species, from sloths and toucans to the quetzal. It makes nearly all its electricity from renewable sources, and its saying "pura vida" sums up its easy-going life.

CUB.a: The largest island of the Caribbean, about 150 km south of Florida. Spain held it for nearly four centuries and made it a land of sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans; it won independence in 1902, after wars against Spain and an American occupation. In 1959 Fidel Castro's revolution took power and built a communist state allied with the Soviet Union, and in 1962 Soviet missiles here brought the world close to nuclear war. Havana's old town and fortresses, the tobacco fields of Viñales and its classic American cars are famous, and its music, from son and rumba to salsa, has travelled the world.
CUB.f: Its bee hummingbird is the smallest bird in the world.

CYP.a: The third-largest island of the Mediterranean, in its far east, near Türkiye and the Levant. Settled by Greeks in ancient times, it was ruled in turn by Persians, Romans, Byzantines, Crusaders, Venetians and Ottomans, then by Britain from 1878 until independence in 1960. Fighting between Greek and Turkish Cypriots, a coup backed by Greece and Türkiye's invasion in 1974 divided the island, and its north declared a state that only Türkiye recognises. The Republic of Cyprus, which holds the south, joined the European Union in 2004. In myth Aphrodite was born from the sea near Paphos, and the island's beaches, mountains and painted Byzantine churches draw visitors from all over Europe.
CYP.f: Its capital, Nicosia, is the last divided capital in Europe.

CZE.a: A landlocked country in Central Europe, made of Bohemia, Moravia and part of Silesia. The Kingdom of Bohemia was among the most powerful in Europe in the 14th century, when Charles IV made Prague the capital of the Holy Roman Empire and founded its university. Later ruled by the Habsburgs, it became part of Czechoslovakia in 1918, was occupied by Nazi Germany and then ruled by communists, until the peaceful Velvet Revolution of 1989. In 1993 Czechoslovakia split peacefully into Czechia and Slovakia. Prague's castle, bridges and spires, the spa town of Karlovy Vary and the castle town of Český Krumlov are among its treasures. Its glass and crystal, and composers such as Dvořák and Smetana, are known worldwide.
CZE.f: Its people drink more beer per head than any other nation.

DEU.a: The most populous country of the European Union, reaching from the North Sea and the Baltic to the Alps. For centuries its lands were a patchwork of states within the Holy Roman Empire, and the birthplace of the printing press and of the Protestant Reformation, begun by Martin Luther in 1517. Prussia united them as the German Empire in 1871. Defeat in the First World War, then Nazi rule, the Holocaust and the Second World War, which it started, led to its division into West and East Germany in 1949. The Berlin Wall fell in 1989, and the country reunited in 1990. Today it is Europe's largest economy, known for its cars and engineering, and a founder of what became the European Union. Bach, Beethoven, Goethe and Einstein were born in its lands, and its castles, half-timbered towns, beer and Christmas markets draw visitors from everywhere.
DEU.f: Most of its rivers flow north to the sea, but the Danube rises in the Black Forest and flows east to the Black Sea.

DJI.a: A small country in the Horn of Africa, on the Bab-el-Mandeb strait, where the Red Sea meets the Gulf of Aden between Africa and Arabia. Once French Somaliland and then the French Territory of the Afars and the Issas, it became independent in 1977. Its port, on one of the world's busiest shipping lanes, is its lifeline, and several foreign powers keep military bases here. Most of its land is hot, dry desert and volcanic rock, crossed by the rifts where Africa is slowly pulling apart. Its people are mostly Somali and Afar, and French and Arabic are its official languages.
DJI.f: Lake Assal, about 155 m below sea level, is the lowest point in Africa and one of the saltiest lakes on Earth.

DMA.a: A mountainous, volcanic island in the Lesser Antilles, between Guadeloupe and Martinique, covered in rainforest. The Kalinago, the island's first people, held out against Europeans longer than on most Caribbean islands, and still live in their own territory on its east coast. Fought over by France and Britain in the 18th century, it was a British colony until independence in 1978. Known as the "nature island", it has hundreds of rivers, waterfalls and hot springs, and sperm whales live off its coast all year.
DMA.f: Its Boiling Lake, a flooded volcanic vent, is the second-largest hot lake in the world.

DNK.a: The southernmost of the Nordic countries, made of the Jutland peninsula and over 400 islands, about 70 of them inhabited, between the North Sea and the Baltic. The Vikings set out from here, and Danish kings once ruled England, Norway and Sweden at different times, and Iceland until 1944. Greenland and the Faroe Islands still belong to the Danish realm, with home rule of their own. It is a constitutional monarchy, among the oldest in the world, and one of the least corrupt and most equal countries on Earth. Hans Christian Andersen, Lego and hygge, its cosy way of life, are known all over the world, and Copenhagen is a city of bicycles.
DNK.f: Its flag, the Dannebrog, is the oldest national flag still in use.

DOM.a: The eastern two-thirds of Hispaniola, which it shares with Haiti, in the Caribbean. Columbus reached the island in 1492, and Santo Domingo, founded in 1496, is the oldest European city in the Americas still inhabited, with the first cathedral and university of the New World. It won independence from Haiti in 1844, and later lived through the long dictatorship of Rafael Trujillo, from 1930 to 1961. Today tourism, mining and money sent home from abroad drive its economy, and its beaches, such as Punta Cana, draw millions. Merengue and bachata were born here, and baseball is a national passion.
DOM.f: Pico Duarte is the highest mountain in the Caribbean.

DZA.a: The largest country in Africa, most of it covered by the Sahara, with a fertile coast on the Mediterranean and the Atlas Mountains between them. Berber (Amazigh) peoples have lived here for millennia; Carthage, Rome, the Arabs and the Ottomans followed. France ruled it from 1830 and made it part of France itself, until a war of independence from 1954 to 1962 that cost hundreds of thousands of lives. Oil and gas, found in the 1950s, are the core of its economy. Arabic and Tamazight are its official languages, and French is widely spoken. Its Roman ruins at Timgad and Djémila, the Kasbah of Algiers and the oasis towns of the Mzab valley are listed by UNESCO.
DZA.f: The rock art of Tassili n'Ajjer, in the Sahara, shows cattle, hunters and rivers from a time when the desert was green.

ECU.a: A country on the equator, which gave it its name, between Colombia and Peru on the Pacific coast. It spans four worlds: the coast, the Andes with their volcanoes, the Amazon rainforest and the Galápagos Islands, whose wildlife helped Charles Darwin form his theory of evolution. Quito was a northern capital of the Inca empire before the Spanish conquest, and its colonial old town was among the first places named a World Heritage Site, in 1978. Independent since 1830, it has used the US dollar as its currency since 2000. It is the world's leading exporter of bananas, and among the largest of shrimp and roses.
ECU.f: Because the Earth bulges at the equator, the summit of Chimborazo is the point on its surface farthest from its centre.

EGY.a: A country of desert crossed by the Nile, along whose valley and delta nearly all its people live. One of the earliest civilisations rose here more than 5,000 years ago, and its pharaohs left the pyramids of Giza, the temples of Luxor and Karnak and the tombs of the Valley of the Kings. Greeks, Romans, Arabs and Ottomans ruled it in turn, and Cairo grew into the largest city of the Arab world. The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, links the Mediterranean to the Red Sea. It became nominally independent from Britain in 1922, and a revolution in 1952 overthrew the monarchy and made it a republic. Arabic is its language, and it is the most populous country in the Arab world.
EGY.f: The Sinai Peninsula puts part of it in Asia, so it lies on two continents.

ERI.a: A country on the Red Sea, in the Horn of Africa, rising from a hot coastal plain to a cool highland plateau. It was part of the ancient Kingdom of Aksum, then an Italian colony from 1890, under British rule after the Second World War, and joined to Ethiopia in 1952. After a thirty-year war it won independence in 1993. It has held no national elections since independence. The Dahlak Archipelago lies off its coast, and Tigrinya, Tigre and Arabic are among its languages.
ERI.f: Its capital, Asmara, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site for its Italian modernist buildings of the 1930s.

ESP.a: A country covering most of the Iberian Peninsula, with the Balearic and Canary Islands, between the Mediterranean and the Atlantic. Phoenicians, Greeks, Romans and Visigoths came before the Moors, who ruled much of it for nearly eight centuries and left the Alhambra of Granada and the Mezquita of Córdoba. The Christian kingdoms completed their reconquest in 1492, the year Columbus sailed for the Americas, and Spain built an empire that spanned the globe. In the 20th century a civil war from 1936 to 1939 led to Franco's dictatorship, followed after his death in 1975 by democracy under a constitutional monarchy. It joined the European Union in 1986. Spanish, the first language of nearly 500 million people, began in Castile, and Catalan, Basque and Galician are also official in their regions. Flamenco, tapas, Gaudí's buildings in Barcelona and the paintings of Velázquez, Goya and Picasso are among its gifts to the world.
ESP.f: It holds two cities in North Africa, Ceuta and Melilla.

EST.a: The northernmost of the three Baltic states, on the Gulf of Finland, with more than 2,000 islands along its coast. Danes, Germans, Swedes and Russians ruled it in turn from the 13th century, until it declared independence in 1918. Occupied by the Soviet Union in 1940, it regained independence in 1991 after the Singing Revolution, when crowds sang for freedom. It joined the European Union and NATO in 2004. It is among the most digital societies in the world, where Skype was created, and about half of its land is forest. Its language, Estonian, is related to Finnish, unlike the languages of its Baltic neighbours, and Tallinn's medieval old town is one of the best preserved in Europe.
EST.f: In 2007 it became the first country to let people vote online in a national election.

ETH.a: A landlocked country in the Horn of Africa, the second most populous in Africa, built on a high plateau split by the Great Rift Valley. Some of the oldest known human ancestors, such as the skeleton called Lucy, were found here. The Kingdom of Aksum, one of the great powers of the ancient world, adopted Christianity in the 4th century, and later kings built the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela and the castles of Gondar. It defeated Italy at the Battle of Adwa in 1896, and apart from an Italian occupation from 1936 to 1941 it was never colonised. The monarchy ended in 1974, and the country has since lived through a Marxist regime, famine and wars. Coffee comes from its highlands, and it keeps a calendar of its own, some seven to eight years behind the Gregorian one.
ETH.f: The Blue Nile, which carries most of the Nile's water, flows out of its Lake Tana.

FIN.a: A country of forests and lakes in northern Europe, between Sweden and Russia, about a quarter of it north of the Arctic Circle. For some 600 years it was part of Sweden, then from 1809 a Grand Duchy of the Russian Empire, and it declared independence in 1917. It held off the Soviet Union in the Winter War of 1939 and 1940, at the cost of land, and stayed neutral during the Cold War. It joined the European Union in 1995 and NATO in 2023. Finnish, related to Estonian and Hungarian, and Swedish are its official languages, and in Lapland the Sámi keep their own. Its schools, its design, from Marimekko to Alvar Aalto, and its heavy metal bands are known far beyond its borders.
FIN.f: It has some 188,000 lakes, and about three million saunas.

FJI.a: An archipelago in the South Pacific, north of New Zealand, whose two largest islands, Viti Levu and Vanua Levu, hold most of its people. Seafaring peoples settled here some 3,000 years ago, and its chiefs ruled until Britain made it a colony in 1874. Britain brought workers from India to its sugar plantations, and their descendants make up about a third of its people. Independent since 1970, it has lived through several coups. Tourism and sugar drive its economy, its coral reefs draw divers, and its rugby sevens team has won Olympic gold.
FJI.f: Only about 110 of its 332 islands are inhabited.

FRA.a: The largest country of the European Union, reaching from the Channel and the North Sea to the Mediterranean, and from the Atlantic to the Rhine and the Alps. Gaul was conquered by Rome, then gave way to the Franks, whose king Charlemagne was crowned emperor in 800. Its kings built Europe's most powerful state, until the Revolution of 1789 proclaimed the rights of man, and Napoleon then ruled much of the continent. It was a battlefield in both world wars, and a founder of what became the European Union. It is the most visited country in the world, for Paris and its Eiffel Tower and Louvre, the castles of the Loire, Mont-Saint-Michel and the Riviera. Its cuisine, wines and cheeses, its fashion and its writers and painters, from Molière to Monet, have shaped Western culture. French is spoken across the world, from Québec to West Africa.
FRA.f: With its lands overseas it spans twelve time zones, more than any other country.

FSM.a: Some 600 islands scattered across the western Pacific, north of the equator, grouped in four states: Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei and Kosrae. Spain, Germany and Japan ruled them in turn, and the United States administered them after the Second World War as a UN trust territory. Independent since 1986, it is in free association with the United States, which handles its defence. On Pohnpei stand the ruins of Nan Madol, a city of stone islets built on a reef some 800 years ago, and Chuuk Lagoon holds dozens of Japanese wrecks from the war.
FSM.f: On Yap, huge carved stone discs called rai are still used as money in traditional exchanges.

GAB.a: A country on the equator, on Africa's Atlantic coast. A French colony, it became independent in 1960, and was ruled by Omar Bongo and then his son from 1967 until a coup in 2023. Oil, manganese and timber have made it one of the wealthier countries of sub-Saharan Africa. About a tenth of its land is set aside in national parks, such as Loango, where elephants walk on the beaches, and Lopé. Its forests also shelter many of the world's western lowland gorillas.
GAB.f: Rainforest covers nearly nine-tenths of the country.

GBR.a: A union of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, on the island of Great Britain, the north-east of Ireland and many smaller islands. England and Scotland were joined under one king in 1603 and as one kingdom in 1707, and Ireland followed in 1801; most of Ireland left in 1922. The first country to industrialise, it built the largest empire in history, covering about a quarter of the world's land around 1920. Its language, English, became the most widely spoken in the world. It stood against Nazi Germany throughout the Second World War, and after the empire's end most of its former colonies joined the Commonwealth. It was a member of the European Union from 1973 to 2020. London, one of the world's great cities, holds Parliament, Buckingham Palace and the Tower of London, and Shakespeare, the Beatles and modern football all come from here.
GBR.f: No place in it is more than 125 km from tidal water.

GEO.a: A country of high mountains and fertile valleys in the South Caucasus, on the Black Sea. In Greek myth Jason sailed to Colchis, on its coast, for the Golden Fleece, and it adopted Christianity in the 4th century. Its medieval kingdom reached its height under Queen Tamar around 1200. Ruled by Persia, the Ottomans and Russia, it was part of the Soviet Union until independence in 1991; Stalin was born here, in Gori. It has its own alphabet and language, unrelated to its neighbours'. Wine has been made here for some 8,000 years, in clay jars called qvevri, and its feasts, the supra, are led by a toastmaster, the tamada.
GEO.f: The two deepest known caves on Earth, both more than 2 km deep, are in its Arabika Massif.

GHA.a: A country on the Gulf of Guinea in West Africa, named after an ancient empire that lay further north. Its Asante kingdom grew rich on gold, which gave the coast its colonial name, the Gold Coast, and European forts along it, such as Elmina and Cape Coast, were used in the Atlantic slave trade. In 1957 it became the first country in sub-Saharan Africa to win independence from colonial rule, led by Kwame Nkrumah. It is one of Africa's most stable democracies, and among the largest producers of gold and cocoa. Kente cloth, highlife music and jollof rice are among its best-known traditions.
GHA.f: Lake Volta, made by a dam in 1965, is the largest artificial lake in the world by area.

GIN.a: A country on the Atlantic coast of West Africa, rising from mangrove coasts to the Fouta Djallon highlands, the water tower of West Africa, where the Gambia and Senegal rivers rise. Part of it once belonged to the Mali Empire. In 1958 it was the only French colony to vote against joining a new French community, and it became independent at once. It holds about a quarter of the world's known bauxite, the ore of aluminium, and the vast Simandou iron ore deposits. Mount Nimba, on its border with Ivory Coast and Liberia, shelters chimpanzees that use stones as tools.
GIN.f: The Niger, West Africa's great river, rises in its highlands.

GMB.a: The smallest country on the African mainland, following the Gambia River inland from the Atlantic, surrounded on every other side by Senegal. Once part of the Mali Empire, it became a British colony, while the land around it became French. Independent since 1965, it formed a short-lived confederation with Senegal in the 1980s. Its river and wetlands are rich in birds, and Kunta Kinteh Island, a slave-trade post in the river, is listed by UNESCO.
GMB.f: Along most of its length it is less than 50 km wide.

GNB.a: A small country on the Atlantic coast of West Africa, of mangroves, rivers and low islands. It was a Portuguese colony from the 15th century, and won independence in 1974 after a war of liberation led by Amílcar Cabral's movement. It has known many coups and much instability since. Most of its people farm, and cashew nuts are by far its main export. Its coast and the islands offshore are rich in birds and in nesting sea turtles.
GNB.f: On its Bijagós Islands, hippos live by the shore and swim in the sea.

GNQ.a: A small country in Central Africa, made of a mainland region, Río Muni, and islands in the Gulf of Guinea, among them Bioko, home to Malabo. It is the only country in Africa with Spanish as an official language, a legacy of Spanish rule until 1968. Oil found offshore in the 1990s made it one of the richest countries in Africa per person. Bioko's forests shelter rare monkeys, and sea turtles nest on its beaches.
GNQ.f: Despite its name, the equator does not pass through it.

GRC.a: A country of mountains, peninsulas and some 6,000 islands at the southern tip of the Balkans, between the Aegean, Ionian and Mediterranean seas. Ancient Greece gave the world democracy, philosophy, theatre and much of Western science, and its temples, from the Parthenon in Athens to Delphi, still stand. After Alexander the Great its culture spread as far as Egypt and India, and it lived on in the Byzantine Empire for a thousand years. Under Ottoman rule for about four centuries, it won independence in the 1820s. It joined the European Community in 1981, and tourism and shipping are pillars of its economy. Santorini, Crete, Mykonos and the monasteries of Meteora on their rock towers are among its many sights.
GRC.f: The Olympic Games began here, at Olympia, in 776 BC.

GRD.a: A small island country in the southern Caribbean, made of Grenada itself, Carriacou, Petite Martinique and some smaller islands. France and Britain fought over it until it became British for good in 1783, and it became independent in 1974. A revolution in 1979 and a coup in 1983 were followed by an invasion led by the United States. Its beaches, such as Grand Anse, and the world's first underwater sculpture park draw visitors.
GRD.f: Known as the Spice Isle, it grows so much nutmeg that one is drawn on its flag.

GTM.a: The most populous country in Central America, a land of volcanoes, highland lakes and rainforest between Mexico and Honduras. It was a heartland of the Maya, and Maya peoples still make up a large share of its population, speaking more than 20 Mayan languages. Spain conquered it in the 1520s, and Antigua Guatemala, its old colonial capital, keeps its baroque churches among the volcanoes. Independent since 1821, it lived through a civil war from 1960 to 1996. Lake Atitlán, ringed by volcanoes and Maya villages, is often called one of the most beautiful lakes in the world, and its coffee and woven textiles are famous.
GTM.f: Tikal, in its northern rainforest, was one of the greatest Maya cities, with temples over 60 m tall.

GUY.a: A country on the north-east coast of South America, the only one on the continent with English as its official language; its name is said to mean "land of many waters". Dutch and then British colonists grew sugar here with enslaved Africans and, after slavery ended, workers from India, whose descendants are now its largest group. Independent since 1966, it is closer to the Caribbean than to Latin America in its culture. Nearly all its people live on the narrow coastal plain, much of it below sea level behind sea walls, while rainforest covers most of the country. Oil found offshore in 2015 has made its economy one of the fastest-growing in the world.
GUY.f: Kaieteur Falls drops about 226 m in a single fall, one of the most powerful waterfalls in the world.

HND.a: A mountainous country in Central America, with a long Caribbean coast and a short one on the Pacific. Spain ruled it from the 16th century until 1821. In the 20th century American fruit companies grew bananas on such a scale here that it became the original "banana republic". The Bay Islands, Roatán and Utila among them, lie on the Mesoamerican Reef and draw divers, and Garifuna communities live along its Caribbean coast. La Mosquitia, in the east, is one of the largest rainforests left in Central America.
HND.f: Copán, in its west, was a great Maya city; its stairway carries the longest Maya inscription known.

HRV.a: A crescent-shaped country between Central Europe and the Adriatic, whose coast is lined with more than a thousand islands and islets. Croats settled here in the 7th century and formed a kingdom that joined Hungary in 1102; later Venice held much of the coast and the Habsburgs the interior. Part of Yugoslavia after the First World War, it declared independence in 1991, which was followed by war until 1995. It joined the European Union in 2013. Dubrovnik's walled old town, Diocletian's Palace in Split and the lakes and waterfalls of Plitvice are among its treasures, and its football team reached the World Cup final in 2018.
HRV.f: The cravat, and so the necktie, is named after Croatian soldiers' scarves, admired in 17th-century Paris.

HTI.a: The western third of Hispaniola, in the Caribbean, which it shares with the Dominican Republic. As the French colony of Saint-Domingue it was the richest in the Caribbean, producing much of the world's sugar and coffee with hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans. Led by Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines, it became independent in 1804, the first black republic and the second independent country in the Americas. Its history since has known foreign occupation, dictatorship, poverty and disasters, among them the earthquake of 2010. Haitian painting, music and the Vodou religion are known far beyond its shores, and the Citadelle Laferrière, a mountain fortress built after independence, is listed by UNESCO. Haitian Creole and French are its official languages.
HTI.f: It is the only country born of a successful slave revolt.

HUN.a: A landlocked country in the Carpathian Basin of Central Europe, crossed by the Danube and the Tisza. The Magyars arrived here in the late 9th century, and Stephen I, crowned in 1000, made it a Christian kingdom. After a century and a half of Ottoman rule, it came under the Habsburgs, and from 1867 shared the dual monarchy of Austria-Hungary. Defeat in the First World War cost it two-thirds of its land. After the Second World War it was a communist state, rising against Soviet rule in 1956, and it joined the European Union in 2004. Its language, Hungarian, is not Indo-European but Uralic, distantly related to Finnish and Estonian. Budapest's Parliament on the Danube, its thermal baths, Lake Balaton, paprika, goulash and Tokaji wine are its best-known sights and tastes.
HUN.f: The Rubik's Cube was invented in Budapest, in 1974.

IDN.a: The largest archipelago country in the world, some 17,000 islands stretching more than 5,000 km along the equator between Asia and Australia. It is the fourth most populous country and has more Muslims than any other, alongside Hindu Bali and many other faiths. Its islands lay on the spice routes for centuries, home to Hindu and Buddhist kingdoms that built Borobudur and Prambanan, before Islam spread and the Dutch made it their colony. It declared independence in 1945, which the Netherlands recognised in 1949 after four years of fighting. It sits on the Ring of Fire, with more active volcanoes than any other country. Its rainforests shelter orangutans, tigers and rhinos, and its hundreds of peoples speak over 700 languages, united by Indonesian.
IDN.f: Komodo dragons, the largest lizards on Earth, live wild on a few of its islands and nowhere else.

IND.a: The most populous country in the world, filling most of the Indian subcontinent, from the Himalayas to the tropical south. The Indus Valley civilisation flourished here some 4,500 years ago, and Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism were all born here. Great empires rose and fell, from the Mauryas and the Guptas to the Mughals, who left the Taj Mahal. Britain took control step by step from the 18th century until independence in 1947, won largely through Mahatma Gandhi's non-violent movement, when the subcontinent was partitioned and Pakistan was created. Since then it has been the world's largest democracy. Its states speak hundreds of languages, with Hindi and English used by the central government. It is now one of the world's largest economies, known for its software industry and for Bollywood, its films. Its food, spices, yoga, cricket and festivals such as Diwali and Holi are loved around the world.
IND.f: Chess began here, around the 6th century, as a game called chaturanga.

IRL.a: An island country in the Atlantic, west of Great Britain, covering most of the island of Ireland. Celtic peoples lived here before Saint Patrick brought Christianity in the 5th century, and its monasteries kept learning alive in Europe's early Middle Ages, producing the Book of Kells. English and then British rule lasted for centuries; the Great Famine of the 1840s killed about a million people and led millions more to emigrate. After a rising in 1916 and a war of independence, most of the island became independent in 1922, while the north-east stayed in the United Kingdom. It joined the European Community in 1973, and its economy boomed as the "Celtic Tiger". Irish, a Celtic language, and English are both official. Writers such as Joyce, Yeats, Wilde and Beckett, its music and its pubs have made it known all over the world.
IRL.f: No snakes are native to the island; legend says Saint Patrick drove them into the sea.

IRN.a: A large country of mountains and deserts between the Caspian Sea and the Persian Gulf, at the heart of one of the world's oldest civilisations. Cyrus the Great founded the Persian Empire in the 6th century BC, the largest the world had yet seen, and its ceremonial capital, Persepolis, still stands in ruins. After the Arab conquest in the 7th century it adopted Islam but kept its language, Persian, and its culture, which flowered in poetry, from Ferdowsi to Hafez. Under the Safavids, from 1501, Shia Islam became its faith, and Isfahan was made one of the most beautiful cities in the world. A revolution in 1979 overthrew the Shah and made it an Islamic republic. It holds some of the world's largest reserves of oil and gas, and its carpets, saffron and pistachios are famous.
IRN.f: Its year begins at the spring equinox, with Nowruz, a festival more than 3,000 years old.

IRQ.a: A country in the Middle East built around the Tigris and Euphrates, the Mesopotamia of the ancient world, where some of the first cities and the first written laws arose. Sumer, Akkad, Babylon and Assyria rose here in turn, and Hammurabi's laws and the legend of the Hanging Gardens of Babylon belong to its past. Baghdad, founded in 762, was the capital of the Abbasid caliphate and one of the greatest cities of the medieval world. After Ottoman rule and a British mandate, it became independent in 1932. Under Saddam Hussein it fought long wars with Iran and over Kuwait, and after the US-led invasion of 2003 it lived through years of conflict. It holds some of the world's largest oil reserves, and the marshes of the south, home to the Marsh Arabs, are listed by UNESCO.
IRQ.f: Cuneiform, one of the first ways of writing, was invented here in Sumer more than 5,000 years ago.

ISL.a: A volcanic island in the North Atlantic, just south of the Arctic Circle, where the Mid-Atlantic Ridge rises above the sea. Norse settlers arrived in the 9th century, and its sagas, written in the Middle Ages, are among the great works of European literature. Ruled by Norway and then Denmark, it became fully independent in 1944. Glaciers, volcanoes, waterfalls and geysers cover its land, among them Geysir, which gave all geysers their name, and nearly all its electricity and heating come from hydropower and geothermal energy. Most of its people live in and around Reykjavík, the northernmost capital of a sovereign state. In winter the northern lights dance over it, and in summer the sun barely sets.
ISL.f: Its parliament, the Althing, has met since 930, which makes it one of the oldest in the world.

ISR.a: A small country on the eastern Mediterranean, reaching from the hills of Galilee to the Negev desert and the Red Sea at Eilat. The land is holy to Judaism, Christianity and Islam, and Jerusalem holds the Western Wall, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and the Dome of the Rock. Ancient Israelite kingdoms stood here, and after centuries of Roman, Arab, Crusader, Ottoman and British rule, the State of Israel was declared in 1948 as a homeland for the Jewish people, after the Holocaust. Its founding and the wars that followed displaced hundreds of thousands of Palestinians, and conflict with them and with its neighbours has marked its history. Hebrew, revived as a spoken language in modern times, is its main language, and it is a world leader in technology.
ISR.f: Mount Sodom, near the Dead Sea, is a hill made mostly of salt, and holds the longest salt cave in the world.

ITA.a: A boot-shaped peninsula reaching into the Mediterranean from the Alps, with the large islands of Sicily and Sardinia. Rome grew from a city on the Tiber into an empire around the whole Mediterranean, and its language, Latin, became the root of the Romance languages. After Rome's fall the peninsula split into city-states and kingdoms, and Florence, Venice and Rome gave birth to the Renaissance, the age of Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael. Italy was unified only in 1861, became a republic in 1946, and was a founder of what became the European Union. It has more World Heritage Sites than almost any other country, from the Colosseum and Pompeii to the canals of Venice and the leaning tower of Pisa. Its food, from pizza and pasta to espresso and gelato, its fashion, its opera and its cars are loved worldwide. Etna and Vesuvius are among Europe's most famous volcanoes.
ITA.f: Two other countries lie entirely inside it: Vatican City and San Marino.

JAM.a: An island in the Caribbean, south of Cuba, whose name comes from the Taíno word for "land of wood and water". Spain held it first, then Britain from 1655, and its sugar plantations were worked by enslaved Africans until slavery ended in the 1830s. Independent since 1962, it has given the world far more than its size suggests: Bob Marley, the sprinters Usain Bolt and Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce, and the Rastafari movement. The Blue Mountains grow one of the world's most prized coffees, and jerk cooking and rum are part of its daily life. Its beaches at Negril and Montego Bay draw visitors from all over the world.
JAM.f: Reggae grew up here in the late 1960s, out of ska and rocksteady.

JOR.a: A country of desert and highland in the Middle East, almost landlocked but for a short coast on the Gulf of Aqaba. Petra, the rose-red city carved into cliffs by the Nabataeans more than 2,000 years ago, is one of the wonders of the world, and the red desert of Wadi Rum has stood in for Mars in films. Part of the Ottoman Empire until the First World War, it became a British mandate and then, in 1946, an independent kingdom ruled by the Hashemite family. It has taken in millions of refugees, from Palestine and later from Iraq and Syria. The Jordan River, where Christians believe Jesus was baptised, runs along its western border.
JOR.f: The shore of the Dead Sea, on its western border, is the lowest land on Earth, more than 400 m below sea level.

JPN.a: An island country in the Pacific off East Asia, made of four main islands, Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu and Shikoku, and thousands of smaller ones. Its emperors claim the oldest unbroken line of any monarchy, though for centuries samurai and shoguns held the real power. From 1639 it closed itself to most foreigners for over two centuries, then modernised at astonishing speed after 1868. After defeat in the Second World War, which ended with the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, it rebuilt itself into one of the world's largest economies, known for its cars, electronics and fast trains. Most of its people live on crowded coastal plains, and greater Tokyo is one of the largest metropolitan areas in the world. Earthquakes and volcanoes are part of life on the Ring of Fire. Kyoto's temples, cherry blossoms, sushi, anime and manga are known everywhere.
JPN.f: Mount Fuji, its highest peak, is a volcano that last erupted in 1707.

KAZ.a: The largest landlocked country in the world, and the ninth largest of all, stretching from the Caspian Sea to the Altai Mountains across endless steppe. Nomadic peoples have herded horses on its steppe for thousands of years. Part of the Russian Empire and then the Soviet Union, it saw nuclear tests at Semipalatinsk and the launch of the first satellite and the first man into space from Baikonur, which Russia still uses. Independent since 1991, it grew rich on oil, gas and uranium, and moved its capital from Almaty to Astana in 1997. Kazakhs and Russians are its largest groups, and both languages are widely spoken.
KAZ.f: The wild ancestors of the apples we eat still grow in its mountains near Almaty.

KEN.a: A country in East Africa, on the Indian Ocean, crossed by the equator and the Great Rift Valley. Fossils found around Lake Turkana make it one of the cradles of humankind. Swahili city-states such as Lamu and Mombasa traded across the ocean for centuries before British rule, and Kenya won independence in 1963, after the Mau Mau uprising. Its savannas, above all the Maasai Mara, hold one of the greatest wildlife spectacles on Earth when the wildebeest cross on their great migration. Its runners have dominated long-distance races for decades, and tea, flowers and tourism drive its economy. Swahili and English are its official languages, and Nairobi is one of Africa's main business hubs.
KEN.f: Mount Kenya, Africa's second-highest peak, stands almost on the equator yet still has glaciers.

KGZ.a: A landlocked, mountainous country in Central Asia, where the Tian Shan covers most of the land. The Silk Road crossed it, and its nomadic Kyrgyz people herded horses and sheep across high pastures, as many still do in summer. Part of the Russian Empire and then the Soviet Union, it became independent in 1991. The Epic of Manas, among the longest poems in the world, is its national treasure. Issyk-Kul, one of the largest mountain lakes on Earth, never freezes despite the cold, and the World Nomad Games have been held on its shores.
KGZ.f: The sun on its flag frames the crown of a yurt, the round felt tent of its nomads.

KHM.a: A country in mainland South-East Asia, around the Mekong and the great lake of Tonlé Sap, which swells several times over in the rainy season. From the 9th to the 15th century the Khmer Empire ruled much of the region from Angkor, whose temples are among the wonders of the world. A French protectorate from 1863, it became independent in 1953. Between 1975 and 1979 the Khmer Rouge regime killed some 1.5 to 2 million people, about a quarter of the population, in the Cambodian genocide. Since then it has rebuilt itself, and rice, garments and tourism drive its economy. Khmer is its language, and most of its people are Theravada Buddhists.
KHM.f: Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument in the world, is pictured on its flag.

KIR.a: Thirty-three coral atolls and islands spread over some 3.5 million km² of the central Pacific, in three groups: the Gilbert, Phoenix and Line Islands. Its name, said "Kiribas", is the local form of "Gilberts", and as the Gilbert Islands it was a British colony until independence in 1979. Most of its land is only a few metres above the sea, so rising seas are a grave threat. Kiritimati, or Christmas Island, is the largest coral atoll in the world by land area, and the Phoenix Islands Protected Area is listed by UNESCO.
KIR.f: It lies in all four hemispheres, and its Line Islands are the first land on Earth to start each new day.

KNA.a: Two volcanic islands in the Leeward Islands of the Caribbean, the smallest country in the Americas. Saint Kitts was the first English colony in the Caribbean, from 1623, and its Brimstone Hill Fortress, the "Gibraltar of the West Indies", is listed by UNESCO. Sugar was its mainstay for three centuries, until the industry closed in 2005, and it became independent in 1983. Nevis was the birthplace of Alexander Hamilton, one of the founders of the United States.
KNA.f: From above, Saint Kitts is shaped like a bat and Nevis like a ball.

KOR.a: The southern half of the Korean Peninsula, between the Yellow Sea and the Sea of Japan (East Sea), with mountains covering most of the land. Korean kingdoms flourished for centuries, the Joseon dynasty ruling from 1392 until Japan annexed the peninsula in 1910. After the Second World War it was divided, and the Korean War of 1950 to 1953 ended in an armistice that still splits it at the Demilitarized Zone. From one of the poorest countries in the world it grew, within a few decades, into a rich democracy and a leader in electronics, cars and shipbuilding. Its pop music, films and dramas, the Korean Wave, are followed worldwide, and kimchi and Korean barbecue have spread just as far. Seoul is one of the largest cities in the world.
KOR.f: Its alphabet, Hangul, was designed on purpose in the 1440s, under King Sejong, so that everyone could learn to read.

KWT.a: A small country at the head of the Persian Gulf, between Iraq and Saudi Arabia, mostly flat desert. It grew as a port of traders, pearl divers and boat builders, ruled by the Al Sabah family since the 18th century, and was a British protectorate until 1961. Oil, found in 1938, made it one of the richest countries in the world. In 1990 Iraq invaded and occupied it, until a US-led coalition drove Iraq out in 1991, when retreating troops set hundreds of its oil wells on fire. The Kuwait Towers, on the shore of its capital, have become its symbol.
KWT.f: Its dinar is the most valuable unit of currency in the world.

LAO.a: The only landlocked country in South-East Asia, a land of mountains and forests along the Mekong. The kingdom of Lan Xang, "a million elephants", ruled it from the 14th century, and its old royal capital, Luang Prabang, with its golden temples and morning procession of monks, is listed by UNESCO. A French protectorate from 1893, it became independent in 1953, and has been a communist state since 1975. During the Vietnam War it became the most heavily bombed country per person in history, and unexploded bombs still lie in its fields. Most of its people are Buddhist, and sticky rice is their everyday food.
LAO.f: The Plain of Jars is scattered with thousands of huge stone jars, made around 2,000 years ago, probably for burials.

LBN.a: A small, mountainous country on the eastern Mediterranean, between Syria and Israel. Its ancient Phoenician ports, Byblos, Sidon and Tyre, traded across the sea, and Byblos is among the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. The cedars of its mountains, prized since antiquity, stand on its flag. Under Ottoman and then French rule, it became independent in 1943, with a system sharing power among its religious communities: Christian, Sunni, Shia and Druze. A civil war from 1975 to 1990 devastated it. Beirut is known for its food, nightlife and universities, and the Roman temples of Baalbek are among the largest ever built.
LBN.f: The Phoenicians who lived here spread the alphabet from which Greek, Latin and most of today's alphabets come.

LBR.a: A country on the Atlantic coast of West Africa, founded in 1822 as a home for freed slaves from the United States. It declared independence in 1847, making it Africa's oldest republic, and it was never colonised; its flag recalls that of the United States. Two civil wars from 1989 to 2003 cost some 250,000 lives, and in 2005 it elected Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, the first woman elected head of state in Africa. Rainforest covers much of its land, home to pygmy hippos, and rubber and iron ore are among its exports.
LBR.f: Its capital, Monrovia, is named after James Monroe, the fifth president of the United States.

LBY.a: A large country in North Africa, nearly all of it Sahara, with most of its people on the Mediterranean coast. Greeks founded Cyrene in its east, Phoenicians the cities of its west, and the Roman ruins of Leptis Magna and Sabratha are among the finest anywhere. Ruled by the Ottomans and then Italy, it became independent as a kingdom in 1951. Oil, found in 1959, made it one of the richest countries in Africa, and in 1969 Muammar Gaddafi seized power, ruling until he was overthrown in 2011; years of conflict followed. The Great Man-Made River carries water from desert aquifers to its coast.
LBY.f: Waw an Namus, a volcano in the middle of the Sahara, holds an oasis of small lakes in its crater.

LCA.a: A volcanic island in the Lesser Antilles of the Caribbean, named, by tradition, after Saint Lucy. France and Britain fought over it so often that it changed hands fourteen times, until Britain kept it in 1814; it became independent in 1979. The Pitons, two steep volcanic peaks rising from the sea, are listed by UNESCO, and near them lies Sulphur Springs, a volcano you can drive into. English is its official language, but most people also speak a French-based creole, Kwéyòl.
LCA.f: With two Nobel Prize winners, Arthur Lewis and Derek Walcott, it has more laureates per person than any other country.

LIE.a: A tiny principality in the Alps, between Switzerland and Austria, on the upper Rhine. It takes its name from the princely family that bought its two lordships in 1699 and 1712, and it became sovereign in 1806, as the Holy Roman Empire broke up. It has had no army since 1868, uses the Swiss franc, and is one of the richest countries in the world, with more registered companies than people. Its industry is a world leader in false teeth, and Vaduz Castle, above the capital, is still the prince's home.
LIE.f: It is one of only two doubly landlocked countries, surrounded only by other landlocked ones: the other is Uzbekistan.

LKA.a: A tear-shaped island in the Indian Ocean, off the southern tip of India. Its Sinhalese kingdoms, founded more than 2,000 years ago, built the great Buddhist cities of Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa and the rock fortress of Sigiriya, and Buddhism has been its main faith ever since. The Portuguese and the Dutch held its coasts, and the British the whole island, as Ceylon, until independence in 1948. A civil war between the government and Tamil separatists lasted from 1983 to 2009. Its tea, grown in the cool hill country, is famous worldwide, and its beaches, elephants and leopards draw visitors.
LKA.f: In 1960 it elected the world's first woman prime minister, Sirimavo Bandaranaike.

LSO.a: A small, mountainous kingdom entirely surrounded by South Africa. Moshoeshoe I founded it in the 1820s by gathering peoples fleeing the wars of the time on his mountain stronghold of Thaba Bosiu, and later sought British protection to keep the Boers out. As Basutoland it was a British protectorate until independence in 1966. Its Basotho people wear woollen blankets and conical straw hats, the mokorotlo, which appears on its flag. Water from its highlands is piped to South Africa's cities, and in winter snow falls on its peaks.
LSO.f: Its lowest point, about 1,400 m above the sea, is higher than the lowest point of any other country.

LTU.a: The largest and southernmost of the three Baltic states. It was the last pagan country in Europe, converting to Christianity only in 1387, and its Grand Duchy, joined with Poland, became one of the largest states in Europe, reaching from the Baltic to the Black Sea. Taken over by the Russian Empire in the late 18th century, it declared independence in 1918, but was occupied by the Soviet Union in 1940. In 1989 its people joined hands with Latvians and Estonians in the Baltic Way, a human chain some 675 km long. It joined the European Union and NATO in 2004. Lithuanian is one of the most archaic living Indo-European languages, and the Curonian Spit, a long strip of dunes, is listed by UNESCO.
LTU.f: It was the first Soviet republic to declare independence, on 11 March 1990.

LUX.a: A small, landlocked country between Belgium, France and Germany, with wooded hills in the north and farmland and vineyards along the Moselle in the south. Its capital grew around a castle of 963, whose fortress became so strong it was called the Gibraltar of the North. Independent since 1839, it was occupied by Germany in both world wars. A founder of what became the European Union, it hosts the EU's Court of Justice and other institutions. Steel made it rich in the 20th century, and banking and finance have made it one of the richest countries in the world per person. Its people speak Luxembourgish, French and German, and nearly half of those living there are foreigners.
LUX.f: It is the only grand duchy left in the world.

LVA.a: The middle one of the three Baltic states, a land of forests, lakes and a long sandy coast on the Baltic Sea. German crusaders conquered it in the 13th century, and Riga, founded in 1201, became a rich Hanseatic port. Later ruled by Poland, Sweden and the Russian Empire, it declared independence in 1918, was occupied by the Soviet Union in 1940, and regained independence in 1991. It joined the European Union and NATO in 2004. Its song and dance festivals, with tens of thousands of singers, are listed by UNESCO, and more than a million of its folk songs, the dainas, have been collected. Latvian, a Baltic language, is related to Lithuanian.
LVA.f: Riga has one of the finest collections of Art Nouveau buildings in the world.

MAR.a: A country in the north-west corner of Africa, on both the Atlantic and the Mediterranean, just across the Strait of Gibraltar from Spain. The Atlas Mountains divide its fertile coast from the Sahara. Amazigh (Berber) peoples have lived here for thousands of years, and Arab and Berber dynasties from the 8th century on built Fez, Marrakesh, Meknes and Rabat, its imperial cities. A French and Spanish protectorate from 1912, it became independent in 1956, and it is ruled by kings of the Alaouite dynasty, in power since the 17th century. Its medinas and souks, its mint tea, couscous and tagines, and its crafts of leather, tiles and carpets draw visitors from all over the world. It holds most of the world's known phosphate reserves.
MAR.f: Al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, founded in 859, is often called the oldest university in the world still teaching.

MCO.a: A tiny city-state on the French Riviera, the second-smallest country in the world and the most densely populated. The Grimaldi family seized its rock in 1297, and has ruled it for most of the centuries since. Its casino at Monte Carlo, opened in the 19th century, made it rich, and today it is a byword for wealth, with no income tax for its residents. Its Grand Prix, raced through its streets since 1929, is the most famous race in motor sport. Fewer than a quarter of its residents are Monégasque citizens.
MCO.f: Its flag, red over white, is the same as Indonesia's but for its shape.

MDA.a: A small, landlocked country between Romania and Ukraine, a land of rolling hills, black soil and vineyards. Its lands were the heart of the medieval principality of Moldavia, whose prince Stephen the Great fought off the Ottomans in the 15th century. The Russian Empire took its eastern half, Bessarabia, in 1812; after a period as part of Romania between the world wars, it became a Soviet republic, and then independent in 1991. Transnistria, a strip east of the Dniester, broke away in 1992, and no member of the United Nations recognises it. Its official language, Romanian, is shared with its western neighbour, and wine is its pride.
MDA.f: The Milestii Mici cellars hold the largest wine collection in the world, along some 200 km of underground tunnels.
