MDG.a: The fourth-largest island in the world, in the Indian Ocean off south-east Africa, which split from Africa some 160 million years ago and from India some 88 million years ago. People came late: sailors from South-East Asia, and later Africans, settled it within the last two thousand years, and Malagasy, its language, is related to the languages of Borneo. The Merina kingdom unified much of the island in the 19th century before France made it a colony in 1896; it became independent in 1960. It is the world's leading producer of vanilla. Most of the world's baobab species grow only here, and the spiny forests of the south and the stone needles of the Tsingy de Bemaraha are found nowhere else.
MDG.f: Around 90% of its plants and animals are found nowhere else, lemurs among them.

MDV.a: Some 1,200 coral islands in 26 atolls, strung across the Indian Ocean south-west of India, only about 200 of them inhabited. Buddhist for centuries, its people converted to Islam in the 12th century, and its sultans ruled under British protection until independence in 1965. Tourism, born here in the 1970s, now drives its economy, with each resort on an island of its own, and tuna fishing is its other mainstay. Its reefs, with manta rays and whale sharks, are among the best places to dive on Earth, and rising seas are a grave threat to its future.
MDV.f: It is the flattest country in the world, its land on average only about 2 m above the sea.

MEX.a: A large country between the United States and Central America, with coasts on the Pacific and the Gulf of Mexico. Great civilisations rose here: the Olmecs, Teotihuacan with its pyramids of the Sun and Moon, the Maya of the south and the Aztecs, whose capital Tenochtitlan stood where Mexico City is today. Spain conquered it in 1521, and it became independent in 1821, then lost about half of its territory to the United States in the 1840s. A revolution from 1910 shaped the modern country. It has the largest Spanish-speaking population in the world, and many Indigenous languages, such as Nahuatl and Maya. Its cuisine, from tacos and mole to chocolate and chillies, is listed by UNESCO, and the Day of the Dead, mariachi music and the art of Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera are famous worldwide. Chichén Itzá, Teotihuacan and the beaches of Cancún draw visitors from everywhere.
MEX.f: Maize was first grown here, some 9,000 years ago, from a wild grass called teosinte.

MHL.a: Twenty-nine coral atolls and five islands in the central Pacific, in two parallel chains. Micronesian navigators settled them some 2,000 years ago or more; Germany, then Japan ruled them, and after the Second World War the United States administered them. Between 1946 and 1958 the United States tested 67 nuclear weapons at Bikini and Enewetak atolls, whose people were moved away, and Bikini is still almost empty. Independent since 1986, in free association with the United States, it has most of its land barely above the sea. Kwajalein, one of the largest atolls in the world, holds a US missile test site.
MHL.f: Its early navigators mapped the ocean swells with charts made of sticks and shells.

MKD.a: A landlocked, mountainous country in the central Balkans, along the valley of the Vardar. Its lands were part of ancient Paeonia and Macedon, then of Rome, Byzantium, the medieval Bulgarian and Serbian states and, for five centuries, the Ottoman Empire. Part of Yugoslavia after the First World War, it became independent peacefully in 1991. A long dispute with Greece over its name ended in 2019, when it became North Macedonia, and it joined NATO in 2020. Ohrid, on its lake, was a centre of Slavic learning in the Middle Ages, said to have had 365 churches, and Macedonian, a South Slavic language, is written in Cyrillic. Mother Teresa was born in Skopje.
MKD.f: Lake Ohrid, on its border with Albania, is one of the oldest lakes in the world, more than a million years old.

MLI.a: A large, landlocked country in West Africa, its north in the Sahara and its south watered by the Niger, whose inland delta floods vast plains each year. It takes its name from the Mali Empire, whose ruler Mansa Musa made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 with so much gold that he upset prices in Cairo. Timbuktu, once a great centre of trade and Islamic learning, still keeps its mud mosques and old manuscripts. A French colony, it became independent in 1960. Its music, from the kora to the desert blues of Ali Farka Touré, is loved worldwide, and the Dogon people live along the cliffs of Bandiagara.
MLI.f: The Great Mosque of Djenné is the largest mud-brick building in the world, and the whole town re-plasters it every year.

MLT.a: A small archipelago in the middle of the Mediterranean, south of Sicily, of which Malta, Gozo and tiny Comino are inhabited. Phoenicians, Romans, Arabs and Normans all held it before the Knights of Saint John made it their home in 1530, held off a great Ottoman siege in 1565 and built its fortified capital, Valletta. Britain ruled it from 1800 until independence in 1964, and its people were awarded the George Cross for their courage under bombing in the Second World War. It joined the European Union in 2004 and is its smallest member. Maltese, the only Semitic language written in the Latin alphabet and an official language of the EU, is spoken alongside English.
MLT.f: Its stone temples, built more than 5,000 years ago, are older than Stonehenge and the pyramids of Egypt.

MMR.a: The largest country of mainland South-East Asia, between India, China and Thailand, around the great Irrawaddy River. Burmese kingdoms built Bagan and later Mandalay, and Theravada Buddhism shapes its life: the gilded Shwedagon Pagoda in Yangon is its most sacred site. Britain conquered it in three wars in the 19th century and ruled it at first as part of India; it became independent in 1948. The army has ruled it for most of the time since 1962, and took power again in a coup in 2021, setting off a civil war. It has more than 100 ethnic groups, and is a leading source of jade and rubies.
MMR.f: Bagan, on the Irrawaddy, still has more than 2,000 Buddhist temples and pagodas from the 11th to 13th centuries.

MNE.a: A small, mountainous country on the Adriatic, whose name means "black mountain". Its rulers, often prince-bishops, kept it largely free of the Ottomans in its mountains, and it was recognised as independent in 1878. It joined Yugoslavia after the First World War and stayed with Serbia until a referendum in 2006 restored its independence. It joined NATO in 2017 and uses the euro. The old towns of Kotor and Budva, the Tara River Canyon, one of the deepest in Europe, and the monastery of Ostrog, built into a cliff, are among its sights.
MNE.f: The Bay of Kotor looks like a fjord, but it is a river canyon drowned by the sea.

MNG.a: A vast, landlocked country between Russia and China, a land of steppe, mountains and the Gobi Desert. In the 13th century Genghis Khan united its tribes and founded the Mongol Empire, the largest contiguous land empire in history, reaching from Korea to Hungary. Later under Chinese Qing rule, it declared independence in 1911, became a communist state allied with the Soviet Union in 1924, and turned to democracy in 1990. About a quarter of its people still live as herders, moving with their gers, the round felt tents, and horses, sheep, goats, camels and yaks far outnumber people. The Naadam festival every summer brings wrestling, horse racing and archery. Dinosaur fossils, Velociraptor among them, have been found in the Gobi.
MNG.f: It is the most sparsely populated country in the world, and its capital, Ulaanbaatar, is the coldest.

MOZ.a: A long country on Africa's south-east coast, facing Madagascar across the Mozambique Channel. Swahili and Arab traders worked its coast for centuries before the Portuguese arrived in 1498 and made Mozambique Island their base; its old stone town is listed by UNESCO. Independent from Portugal since 1975, after a ten-year war, it then suffered a civil war until 1992. The Zambezi crosses it to the sea, held back by the great Cahora Bassa dam. Its coast of beaches, coral reefs and islands, such as the Bazaruto Archipelago, is home to dugongs, whale sharks and manta rays. Portuguese is its official language, alongside many Bantu languages.
MOZ.f: Its flag is the only one in the world with a modern rifle on it.

MRT.a: A large country in north-west Africa, on the Atlantic, where the Sahara meets the Sahel; desert covers most of its land. Its people are Arab-Berber Moors and Black Africans, and many once lived as nomads. Its old caravan towns, such as Chinguetti and Ouadane, kept libraries of manuscripts and were centres of learning on the routes across the desert. A French colony, it became independent in 1960. Its iron ore travels to the coast on one of the longest and heaviest trains in the world, and the Banc d'Arguin, off its coast, is a haven for millions of migrating birds.
MRT.f: The Richat Structure, the "Eye of the Sahara", is a ring of rock some 40 km wide, easy to see from space.

MUS.a: A volcanic island in the Indian Ocean, east of Madagascar, ringed by coral reefs and lagoons. Uninhabited until the Dutch settled it in 1638, it was then held by France and, from 1810, Britain, who brought workers from India to its sugar plantations after slavery ended; their descendants are now most of its people. Independent since 1968, it has become one of Africa's most stable and prosperous democracies. Its people speak Mauritian Creole, French and English, and Hindu, Christian and Muslim festivals all fill its calendar. Le Morne, a mountain where escaped slaves took refuge, is listed by UNESCO, as is the Aapravasi Ghat, where indentured workers landed.
MUS.f: It was the only home of the dodo, a flightless bird gone by the end of the 17th century.

MWI.a: A narrow, landlocked country in south-east Africa, along the Great Rift Valley and the long lake that fills much of it. As Nyasaland it was a British protectorate, a land David Livingstone helped open to missions, until independence in 1964. Most of its people farm, and tobacco, tea and sugar are its main exports. It is known as "the warm heart of Africa" for the friendliness of its people. Its national parks, such as Liwonde and Majete, have brought back elephants, rhinos and lions.
MWI.f: Lake Malawi has more species of fish than any other lake on Earth.

MYS.a: A country in two parts, on the Malay Peninsula and in the north of Borneo, separated by the South China Sea. Melaka grew into a great trading port in the 15th century, then fell to the Portuguese, the Dutch and the British, who ruled the peninsula and later Sabah and Sarawak. Malaya became independent in 1957 and formed Malaysia in 1963, which Singapore left two years later. Malays, Chinese and Indians, and many Indigenous peoples of Borneo, live side by side, and its food mixes all their traditions. Tin, rubber and palm oil made it rich, and today electronics and services do. Kuala Lumpur's Petronas Towers were the tallest buildings in the world from 1998 to 2004, and Borneo's rainforests, home to orangutans, are among the oldest on Earth.
MYS.f: Its rainforests grow the Rafflesia, the largest single flower on Earth, which smells of rotting meat.

NAM.a: A large, dry country on Africa's south-west coast, between the Namib and the Kalahari deserts. A German colony from 1884, it saw the genocide of the Herero and Nama peoples from 1904 to 1908, then was ruled by South Africa from 1915. After a long struggle it won independence in 1990. It is one of the least densely populated countries in the world, and among the first to write protection of the environment into its constitution. The red dunes of Sossusvlei, the shipwrecks of the Skeleton Coast and Etosha's salt pan, where animals gather at waterholes, are among its wonders. Its desert-adapted elephants and lions roam where little else lives.
NAM.f: The Namib is thought to be the oldest desert in the world, dry for at least 55 million years.

NER.a: A large, landlocked country in West Africa, most of it in the Sahara, named after the Niger River that crosses its south-west, where most of its people live. Empires such as Songhai and Kanem-Bornu ruled parts of it, and Agadez, with its towering mud-brick minaret, was a gateway for caravans across the desert. A French colony, it became independent in 1960. It has one of the youngest and fastest-growing populations in the world. It is a major producer of uranium, and the Aïr Mountains and the Ténéré desert hold dinosaur fossils and ancient rock art.
NER.f: The Ténéré Tree was once the most isolated tree on Earth, alone in the desert, until a truck knocked it down in 1973.

NGA.a: The most populous country in Africa, on the Gulf of Guinea, where the Niger and Benue rivers meet. Its lands saw the Nok culture's terracotta figures more than 2,000 years ago, and later the kingdoms of Benin, Oyo and Kano; the Benin Bronzes are among Africa's great works of art. Britain joined its north and south into one colony in 1914, and it became independent in 1960. A civil war over the breakaway state of Biafra, from 1967 to 1970, cost over a million lives. Its hundreds of peoples, the largest the Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo, speak more than 500 languages, with English as the official one. Oil made it one of Africa's largest economies, and Lagos is one of the largest cities on the continent. Its Afrobeats music has conquered the world.
NGA.f: Its film industry, Nollywood, makes more films a year than any other but India's.

NIC.a: The largest country in Central America, between Honduras and Costa Rica, with lakes and volcanoes along its Pacific side and rainforest towards the Caribbean. Spain founded Granada and León in 1524, and it became independent in 1821. In the 20th century it lived through American occupation, the Somoza family's dictatorship, a revolution in 1979 and a war in the 1980s. Lake Nicaragua, the largest in Central America, holds the volcanic island of Ometepe, and the Masaya volcano has a lava lake you can look into. Its Caribbean coast is home to Miskito and Creole communities, who speak English and their own languages.
NIC.f: Bull sharks swim up the San Juan River from the Caribbean into Lake Nicaragua.

NLD.a: A small, flat and densely populated country on the North Sea, on the deltas of the Rhine, the Meuse and the Scheldt. After revolting against Spain in 1568, the Dutch Republic grew into the world's leading trading power in the 17th century, its Golden Age, when Rembrandt and Vermeer painted and its ships sailed from New Amsterdam to Indonesia. Its people have spent centuries reclaiming land from the sea as polders, and the Delta Works and the Afsluitdijk now hold the sea back. It was a founder of what became the European Union, and The Hague hosts the International Court of Justice. Windmills, tulips, cheese and bicycles, which outnumber its people, are its symbols, and Amsterdam's canals are listed by UNESCO. Its port, Rotterdam, is the largest in Europe.
NLD.f: About a quarter of it lies below sea level, kept dry by dikes, dunes and pumps.

NOR.a: A long, mountainous country on the west of the Scandinavian Peninsula, its coast cut by deep fjords and reaching far north of the Arctic Circle. The Vikings sailed from here, reaching Iceland, Greenland and North America. It was joined with Denmark for some four centuries and with Sweden from 1814, before becoming fully independent in 1905. Oil and gas found in the North Sea in 1969 made it one of the richest countries in the world, and it saves the profits in the world's largest sovereign wealth fund. In the north the Sámi keep their own language and reindeer herding, the midnight sun shines in summer and the northern lights in winter. It is the home of modern skiing, and has won more Winter Olympic medals than any other country.
NOR.f: With all its fjords and islands, its coast is long enough to wrap around the Earth twice.

NPL.a: A landlocked country in the Himalayas, between China and India, home to eight of the world's ten highest mountains, Everest among them. Lumbini, in its south, was the birthplace of the Buddha, and Hindu and Buddhist temples fill the Kathmandu Valley, whose old royal cities are listed by UNESCO. Prithvi Narayan Shah unified it in the 18th century, and it was never colonised. A civil war ended in 2006, and in 2008 it abolished its monarchy and became a republic. Its Sherpa people are famed as mountaineers, and its Gurkha soldiers have served in the British and Indian armies for two centuries.
NPL.f: Its flag, two stacked triangles, is the only national flag that is not a rectangle.

NRU.a: A single raised coral island in the central Pacific, just south of the equator, the third-smallest country in the world. Germany, then Australia on behalf of Britain and New Zealand, and Japan during the Second World War ruled it before independence in 1968. Phosphate, laid down over ages from the droppings of seabirds, made its people among the richest in the world in the 1970s and 1980s, but mining left most of the island a wasteland of coral pinnacles. Most of its people live on the narrow coastal strip that rings it.
NRU.f: It has no official capital; the government sits in the district of Yaren.

NZL.a: An island country in the south-west Pacific, made of the North Island, the South Island and many smaller ones. It was one of the last lands on Earth to be settled, by Polynesian Māori around 1300, and Māori culture, the haka among it, remains central to its identity. The Treaty of Waitangi, signed with Māori chiefs in 1840, made it a British colony, and it became fully independent step by step in the 20th century. Its landscapes, from the Southern Alps and fjords to volcanoes and geysers, served as Middle-earth in the Lord of the Rings films. Sheep outnumber people, and its kiwi, a flightless bird, gave New Zealanders their nickname. Its rugby team, the All Blacks, is one of the most successful in sport.
NZL.f: In 1893 it became the first self-governing country where women could vote in national elections.

OMN.a: A country on the south-east corner of the Arabian Peninsula, facing the Arabian Sea and the Gulf of Oman, with the Strait of Hormuz at its northern tip. Its frankincense was traded across the ancient world, and its sailors and merchants built an empire reaching to East Africa and the coast of today's Pakistan. From 1970 Sultan Qaboos turned it from one of the most isolated countries in the world into a modern state, while keeping its traditions. Its rugged Hajar Mountains, desert dunes and forts, such as Nizwa and Bahla, draw visitors, and in summer monsoon rains turn the Dhofar region green.
OMN.f: In the 19th century its sultans also ruled Zanzibar, off East Africa, and moved their capital there.

PAK.a: A country in South Asia, reaching from the Arabian Sea to the high Karakoram and Himalaya. The Indus Valley civilisation built Mohenjo-daro and Harappa here more than 4,000 years ago, and later Persian, Greek, Buddhist and Mughal rulers left their mark, from Taxila to Lahore's Badshahi Mosque. It was created in 1947, when British India was partitioned, as a homeland for its Muslims, and its eastern wing became Bangladesh in 1971. It is the fifth most populous country in the world. The Indus and its tributaries water the farmland of Punjab, one of the largest irrigation systems in the world. Cricket is a national passion, and Urdu and English are its official languages, alongside Punjabi, Pashto, Sindhi and Balochi.
PAK.f: K2, the second-highest mountain on Earth, rises on its border with China.

PAN.a: The narrow isthmus that joins Central and South America, between the Caribbean and the Pacific. Spain made it a crossroads for the gold and silver of Peru, carried overland between its two coasts. Part of Colombia after independence from Spain, it broke away in 1903 with American support, and the United States then built the Panama Canal, opened in 1914, which it handed over to Panama in 1999. The canal, widened with new locks in 2016, carries about 5% of the world's sea trade, and banking and shipping make Panama City a hub. Beyond the city lie rainforests, the islands of Guna Yala, home to the Guna people, and the Darién Gap, where the Pan-American Highway stops.
PAN.f: Because the isthmus bends, the canal's Pacific entrance lies east of its Atlantic one.

PER.a: A country on the Pacific coast of South America, from a desert coast across the high Andes to the Amazon rainforest, which covers more than half its land. Caral, near its coast, is among the oldest cities in the Americas, and later cultures left the Nazca Lines and the adobe city of Chan Chan. From Cusco the Inca ruled the largest empire of the Americas, until Spain conquered it in the 1530s; their mountain city of Machu Picchu is one of the wonders of the world. Lima became the capital of Spain's South American empire, and Peru declared independence in 1821. Many of its people speak Quechua or Aymara, and its cuisine, from ceviche to thousands of kinds of potato, is among the most celebrated in the world. Lake Titicaca lies on its border with Bolivia.
PER.f: The Amazon begins as meltwater on the slopes of Nevado Mismi, in the Andes of southern Peru.

PHL.a: An archipelago of more than 7,000 islands in the western Pacific, between Taiwan and Borneo, grouped around Luzon, the Visayas and Mindanao. Magellan arrived in 1521, and Spain ruled it for over three centuries and named it after King Philip II, and it is now the largest mostly Christian country in Asia. After a revolution against Spain in 1896, the United States took it over in 1898, and it became independent in 1946. Its people speak Filipino and English, with more than 170 other languages, and millions work abroad. It sits on the Ring of Fire, with active volcanoes such as Mayon, and typhoons strike it every year. The rice terraces of the Cordilleras, the beaches of Palawan and Boracay and the Chocolate Hills of Bohol are among its wonders.
PHL.f: Its jeepneys, the brightly painted buses of its streets, began as US Army jeeps left behind after the Second World War.

PLW.a: Some 340 islands in the western Pacific, east of the Philippines, of which only a few are inhabited. Its people, who arrived at least 3,000 years ago, came under Spanish, German and Japanese rule; fierce battles were fought on Peleliu in 1944, and the United States administered it after the war. Independent since 1994, it is in free association with the United States. The Rock Islands, hundreds of green limestone domes rising from a turquoise lagoon, are listed by UNESCO, and Jellyfish Lake is filled with millions of golden jellyfish with only a mild sting. Visitors must sign a pledge, stamped in their passport, to protect its nature.
PLW.f: In 2009 it made its waters the world's first shark sanctuary.

PNG.a: The eastern half of New Guinea, the world's second-largest island, with hundreds of smaller islands, just north of Australia. People have lived here for at least 50,000 years, and farmers in its highlands, at Kuk, were among the first in the world to grow crops, some 7,000 to 10,000 years ago. The highland valleys were unknown to outsiders until the 1930s, when explorers found about a million people living there. Germany and Britain divided it in 1884, and Australia ran all of it from the First World War until independence in 1975. Most of its people live in rural villages, on land held by their clans. Its rainforests and coral reefs are among the richest on Earth, home to birds of paradise and tree kangaroos.
PNG.f: More than 800 languages are spoken there, more than in any other country.

POL.a: A country of the North European Plain, reaching from the Baltic coast to the Carpathian and Sudeten mountains. Its history as a state begins in 966, when its ruler Mieszko I was baptised, and in union with Lithuania it later became one of the largest states of Europe. Partitioned by Russia, Prussia and Austria in the late 18th century, it vanished from the map for 123 years, until it was reborn in 1918. In 1939 the Second World War began with its invasion by Germany and the Soviet Union; the war killed about a sixth of its people, among them some three million Polish Jews, and Nazi Germany built Auschwitz and other death camps on its occupied land. After decades of communist rule, the Solidarity movement led it to democracy in 1989, and it joined NATO in 1999 and the European Union in 2004. Copernicus and Chopin were born here, and Kraków's old town and the Wieliczka salt mine are among its treasures.
POL.f: Marie Curie, born in Warsaw, was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes.

PRK.a: The northern half of the Korean Peninsula, a land of mountains between China, Russia and South Korea. Japan ruled all of Korea from 1910 to 1945; after the Second World War the north came under Soviet control, and Kim Il Sung founded a communist state in 1948. Its invasion of the south began the Korean War, which ended in 1953 with an armistice but no peace treaty. The Kim family has ruled it ever since, under an ideology of self-reliance called Juche, and it is one of the most closed and tightly controlled countries in the world. It has built nuclear weapons despite international sanctions. Pyongyang is a showcase of monuments and wide avenues.
PRK.f: Mount Paektu, on its border with China, erupted around the year 946 in one of the largest eruptions in recorded history.

PRT.a: A country on the western edge of the Iberian Peninsula, facing the Atlantic, with the Azores and Madeira out in the ocean. It became a kingdom in the 12th century, and in the 15th and 16th centuries its sailors led Europe's age of discovery: Vasco da Gama reached India by sea, Cabral reached Brazil, and it built an empire from Brazil to Macau. Lisbon was largely destroyed by an earthquake and tsunami in 1755. The peaceful Carnation Revolution ended a long dictatorship in 1974, and it joined the European Community in 1986. Fado, its soulful song, port wine from the Douro valley and the blue and white tiles called azulejos are its signatures, and the beaches of the Algarve draw visitors from all over Europe.
PRT.f: Its border with Spain, set in 1297, is one of the oldest in the world.

PRY.a: A landlocked country in the heart of South America, divided by the Paraguay River into the wetter east and the dry Chaco in the west. Jesuit missions organised Guarani communities here in the 17th and 18th centuries, and their ruins, such as Trinidad, are listed by UNESCO. Independent since 1811, it lost a huge share of its people in the War of the Triple Alliance against Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay, from 1864 to 1870, and fought Bolivia over the Chaco in the 1930s. The Itaipú dam, which it shares with Brazil, is one of the largest hydroelectric plants in the world and makes most of Paraguay's electricity. Its people drink tereré, a cold version of mate.
PRY.f: Guarani, the language of its first peoples, is spoken by most Paraguayans and is official beside Spanish.

QAT.a: A small peninsula jutting north into the Persian Gulf from Arabia, mostly flat, dry desert. Pearl diving and fishing sustained it until oil was found in 1939; it has been ruled by the Al Thani family since the 19th century, and became independent from British protection in 1971. Its natural gas, from the largest field in the world, which it shares with Iran, has made it one of the richest countries in the world per person. Most people living there are foreign workers. Doha's skyline, the Museum of Islamic Art and the stadiums of the 2022 World Cup, the first held in the Arab world, are among its landmarks.
QAT.f: Its maroon flag is the only national flag more than twice as wide as it is tall.

ROU.a: A country in south-eastern Europe, ringed by the Carpathian Mountains, with a coast on the Black Sea. Its people trace their roots to the Dacians and to the Romans who conquered them in 106, and Romanian is the only major Romance language of Eastern Europe. The principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia united in 1859 and became independent in 1878, and Transylvania joined them in 1918. After the Second World War it was a communist state, until a revolution in 1989 overthrew Nicolae Ceaușescu. It joined NATO in 2004 and the European Union in 2007. Transylvania's castles, such as Bran, linked with the legend of Dracula, the painted monasteries of Bukovina and the Danube Delta, one of Europe's largest wetlands, are among its treasures.
ROU.f: The Palace of the Parliament in Bucharest is the heaviest building in the world.

RUS.a: The largest country in the world, covering much of Eastern Europe and all of northern Asia, across eleven time zones. The princes of Moscow, who threw off Mongol rule in 1480, built a state that grew under the tsars into an empire from the Baltic to the Pacific. Peter the Great opened it to the West and founded Saint Petersburg in 1703. The revolution of 1917 brought the Bolsheviks to power and made it the heart of the Soviet Union, which lost some 27 million people in the Second World War and became a superpower, sending the first satellite and the first human into space. The Soviet Union broke up in 1991; in 2014 Russia annexed Crimea, and in 2022 it launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. It is rich in oil, gas, timber and minerals, and Siberia's taiga is part of the largest forest on Earth. Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, Tchaikovsky and the Bolshoi Ballet are among its gifts to the world, and the Kremlin and Red Square stand at the heart of Moscow.
RUS.f: Lake Baikal, in Siberia, holds about a fifth of the fresh water in all the world's lakes and rivers.

RWA.a: A small, landlocked country of green hills in the Great Lakes region of Africa, called the land of a thousand hills. A kingdom for centuries, it came under German and then Belgian rule, which hardened the divide between Hutu and Tutsi, and it became independent in 1962. In 1994, in about a hundred days, hundreds of thousands of people, most of them Tutsi, were murdered in the genocide against the Tutsi. Since then it has rebuilt itself into one of Africa's fastest-growing economies. Its mountain gorillas, in the volcanoes of the Virunga range, draw visitors from all over the world.
RWA.f: It banned plastic bags in 2008, and on the last Saturday of each month people work together to clean their towns.

SAU.a: The largest country of the Arabian Peninsula, most of it desert, including the Rub' al Khali, the largest continuous sand desert in the world. Islam was born here in the 7th century: Mecca, the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad, and Medina are its holiest cities, and millions of pilgrims come every year for the Hajj. The Al Saud family united most of the peninsula and founded the kingdom in 1932. Oil, found in 1938, made it one of the world's largest producers and exporters, and one of its richest countries. Since 2016 it has begun to open up to tourism and entertainment, and the Nabataean tombs of Hegra, at AlUla, are among its sights. Arabic is its language, and its laws are based on Islam.
SAU.f: It is the largest country in the world without a river.

SDN.a: A large country in north-east Africa, where the Blue and White Niles meet at Khartoum. The kingdom of Kush ruled here, and for a time over Egypt too, as its 25th dynasty of pharaohs. Christian kingdoms followed, then Islamic sultanates, and from 1899 joint British and Egyptian rule, until independence in 1956. Long civil wars between north and south led to South Sudan's independence in 2011, and Darfur in the west saw mass killings in the 2000s. A war that broke out in 2023 has driven millions from their homes. Most of its people are Arabic-speaking Muslims, alongside many other peoples and languages.
SDN.f: It has more pyramids than Egypt, built by the kings of Kush at Meroe and elsewhere.

SEN.a: The westernmost country of mainland Africa, on the Atlantic, where Dakar sits on the Cap-Vert peninsula. Parts of it belonged to the empires of Ghana and Mali, and its Wolof kingdoms traded with Europeans on the coast. Gorée Island, off Dakar, became a symbol of the Atlantic slave trade, and Saint-Louis was the first capital of French West Africa. Independent since 1960, it is one of Africa's most stable democracies and has never had a military coup; its first president, Léopold Sédar Senghor, was a celebrated poet. Most of its people are Muslim, many in Sufi brotherhoods such as the Mourides, whose holy city is Touba, and its music, mbalax, and teranga, its spirit of hospitality, are its pride.
SEN.f: Lake Retba, near Dakar, is pink, coloured by algae in its very salty water.

SGP.a: A city-state on an island at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula, on one of the world's busiest sea lanes. Stamford Raffles founded a British trading post here in 1819, and it grew into a great port. Occupied by Japan in the Second World War, it joined Malaysia in 1963 but left two years later to become independent. Under Lee Kuan Yew it turned from a poor port into one of the richest countries in the world, a hub of finance, trade and shipping. Its Chinese, Malay and Indian communities live side by side, with English, Mandarin, Malay and Tamil as official languages. It is famous for its order and cleanliness, its hawker food centres and its gardens, from the Botanic Gardens to the Supertrees of Gardens by the Bay.
SGP.f: Land won from the sea has made it about a quarter larger than it was in the 1960s.

SLB.a: A double chain of nearly a thousand islands in the south-west Pacific, east of Papua New Guinea. Melanesian peoples have lived here for thousands of years, and Britain made it a protectorate in the 1890s. In 1942 and 1943 Guadalcanal was the scene of one of the fiercest campaigns of the Pacific war. Independent since 1978, it went through years of ethnic unrest from 1998 to 2003. Most of its people live in villages and speak some 70 languages, linked by Solomons Pijin, and its seas hold coral reefs and wrecks from the war.
SLB.f: Rennell Island, a raised coral atoll, holds Lake Tegano, the largest lake of the Pacific islands.

SLE.a: A country on the Atlantic coast of West Africa, of mangrove coasts, forested hills and plateaus. Freetown was founded in 1792 as a home for freed slaves, among them Black Loyalists from North America, and became a British colony. Their descendants, the Krio, gave the country its common language, Krio. Independent since 1961, it suffered a brutal civil war from 1991 to 2002, fuelled by diamonds, and an Ebola epidemic from 2014 to 2016. Its beaches, the primates of Tiwai Island and the chimpanzee sanctuary of Tacugama are among its sights.
SLE.f: Its name comes from the Portuguese for "lion mountains", given to the hills around Freetown in 1462.

SLV.a: The smallest and most densely populated country of mainland Central America, and the only one without a Caribbean coast. Its land is a chain of volcanoes along the Pacific, with fertile soil that made it a land of coffee. It became independent from Spain in 1821, and a civil war from 1980 to 1992 cost some 75,000 lives. In 2001 it adopted the US dollar, and in 2021 it was the first country to make Bitcoin legal tender, a step it scaled back in 2025. Pupusas, stuffed corn tortillas, are its national dish, and its Pacific coast is known for surfing.
SLV.f: Joya de Cerén, a farming village buried by volcanic ash around the year 600, is called the Pompeii of the Americas.

SMR.a: A tiny, landlocked republic on the slopes of Monte Titano, entirely surrounded by Italy. By tradition it was founded in 301 by Marinus, a Christian stonemason who fled persecution, and it kept its independence even through Italy's unification. Its three towers, perched on the cliffs, appear on its coat of arms and flag, and its historic centre is listed by UNESCO. It is led by two Captains Regent, elected every six months. Tourism, banking and its postage stamps and coins, prized by collectors, support its economy.
SMR.f: It claims to be the oldest republic in the world still standing.

SOM.a: A country on the Horn of Africa with the longest coastline of mainland Africa, on the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. Its ports traded with Arabia, Persia and India for centuries, and Mogadishu was a rich trading city in the Middle Ages. Divided between British and Italian rule, its two parts united at independence in 1960. Since the fall of its government in 1991 it has suffered civil war, famine and insurgency, and Somaliland in the north has declared itself independent, though most countries do not recognise it. Most Somalis share one language, Somali, and one faith, Islam, and herding is a way of life: it has more camels than any other country.
SOM.f: It is often called a nation of poets, for the place verse holds in everyday life.

SRB.a: A landlocked country in the central Balkans, where the Pannonian plain of the north meets the mountains of the south, crossed by the Danube and the Sava, which meet at Belgrade. The medieval Serbian kingdom of the Nemanjić dynasty built monasteries such as Studenica, but fell to the Ottomans after the Battle of Kosovo in 1389 and the fall of Smederevo in 1459. Uprisings in 1804 and 1815 began its road to independence, recognised in 1878. It was the core of Yugoslavia from 1918, and after the wars of the 1990s that broke Yugoslavia up, it became a separate state again in 2006. Kosovo declared independence from it in 2008, which Serbia does not recognise. Belgrade, one of the oldest cities in Europe, is known for its nightlife, and Serbian is written in both Cyrillic and Latin letters.
SRB.f: Nikola Tesla's ashes are kept in a golden sphere at his museum in Belgrade.

SSD.a: The world's youngest country, a landlocked land of savanna, swamp and forest in east-central Africa, crossed by the White Nile. Its peoples, among them the Dinka, Nuer and Shilluk, are mostly herders and farmers, for whom cattle are wealth. Ruled with Sudan by Britain and Egypt, it fought two long civil wars against the north before voting for independence in 2011, and a civil war from 2013 to 2018 followed. Each year one of the largest animal migrations on Earth, of antelopes such as the white-eared kob, crosses its plains.
SSD.f: The Sudd, a swamp of the White Nile, can spread over a seventh of the country in the rainy season.

STP.a: Two volcanic islands in the Gulf of Guinea, off the coast of Gabon, the second-smallest country in Africa. Uninhabited until the Portuguese arrived around 1470, they became a hub of sugar and the slave trade, then of cocoa, of which they were for a time the world's largest producer. Independent since 1975, it has been a multiparty democracy since 1991. Its rainforests, below dramatic volcanic peaks such as the Pico Cão Grande, shelter birds and plants found nowhere else, and Príncipe is a UNESCO biosphere reserve.
STP.f: The equator crosses the islet of Rolas, just off São Tomé's southern tip.

SUR.a: The smallest country in South America, on its north-east coast, with rainforest covering more than nine-tenths of its land. Dutch planters grew sugar here with enslaved Africans, some of whom escaped into the forest and founded the Maroon communities that still live there. After slavery ended in 1863, workers came from India, Java and China, making its people among the most diverse in the world. Independent since 1975, it is the only independent country in the Americas with Dutch as its official language, and Sranan Tongo is its common tongue. Its Central Suriname Nature Reserve is one of the largest protected tropical forests on Earth.
SUR.f: In 1667 the Dutch kept it in exchange for New Amsterdam, today's New York.

SVK.a: A landlocked country in Central Europe, mountainous in the north, where the High Tatras rise, and fertile along the Danube in the south. For a thousand years its lands were part of the Kingdom of Hungary, and Bratislava, then known as Pressburg or Pozsony, was where Hungary's kings were crowned for more than 250 years. It joined the Czechs in Czechoslovakia in 1918, lived under communism after the Second World War, and became independent peacefully in 1993. It joined NATO and the European Union in 2004, and uses the euro. It has hundreds of castles and castle ruins, Spiš Castle among the largest in Central Europe, and its caves are among the finest in Europe.
SVK.f: It makes more cars per person than any other country.

SVN.a: A small country where the Alps, the Pannonian plain, the Dinaric karst and the Adriatic meet, with a short coast on the Gulf of Trieste. For centuries its lands were ruled by the Habsburgs, and it was part of Yugoslavia from 1918. It became independent in 1991 after a ten-day war, and joined the European Union and NATO in 2004. More than half of its land is forest, and Lake Bled, with its island church, and the Škocjan and Postojna caves are among its sights. Its Kras plateau gave its name to karst, the landscape of limestone caves and sinkholes.
SVN.f: Its caves are home to the olm, a blind salamander that can live for a hundred years.

SWE.a: The most populous Nordic country, on the eastern side of the Scandinavian Peninsula, from the Baltic to the mountains along Norway, with forests covering most of its land. Vikings sailed east from here, down the rivers of what are now Russia and Ukraine, and in the 17th century Sweden was a great power ruling much of the Baltic. It has not fought a war since 1814 and stayed neutral in both world wars, before joining the European Union in 1995 and NATO in 2024. It is known for its welfare state, its design, companies such as IKEA, Volvo and Spotify, and pop music from ABBA onwards. Alfred Nobel founded the Nobel Prizes, most of them awarded in Stockholm every December. In the far north, where the midnight sun shines in summer, Sámi herders keep reindeer.
SWE.f: Under the "everyman's right", anyone may walk, camp and pick berries on almost any land.

SWZ.a: A small, landlocked kingdom in southern Africa, between South Africa and Mozambique, known as Swaziland until 2018. The Swazi nation took shape in the 18th and 19th centuries, kept its king under British protection, and became independent in 1968. Its culture is alive in great ceremonies such as the Umhlanga, the reed dance, and the Incwala, the kingship ceremony. Its landscapes range from highland forest to lowland bush, where reserves such as Hlane shelter rhinos, elephants and lions.
SWZ.f: It is the last absolute monarchy in Africa.

SYC.a: An archipelago of 115 islands in the Indian Ocean, north-east of Madagascar, the smallest country in Africa. Uninhabited until the 18th century, it was settled by the French with enslaved Africans, passed to Britain in 1814 and became independent in 1976. Its granite islands, such as Mahé, Praslin and La Digue, are rare among ocean islands, and Aldabra, one of the largest coral atolls in the world, is home to some 100,000 giant tortoises. Tourism and tuna fishing drive its economy, and its people speak Seychellois Creole, English and French.
SYC.f: The coco de mer, a palm of its islands, grows the largest seed in the world.

SYR.a: A country on the eastern Mediterranean, between Türkiye, Iraq, Jordan, Israel and Lebanon, much of it steppe and desert, crossed by the Euphrates. Some of the world's first farmers lived here, and Ugarit, on its coast, used one of the first alphabets. Aleppo grew rich on the trade routes between the Mediterranean and the East, and Palmyra, a caravan city of the desert, flourished under Rome. Damascus was the capital of the Umayyad caliphate, whose Great Mosque still stands. After Ottoman rule and a French mandate it became independent in 1946, and the Assad family ruled it from 1970 until 2024. A civil war that began in 2011 killed hundreds of thousands of people and forced millions to flee.
SYR.f: Damascus, its capital, is thought to be one of the oldest cities in the world still lived in.

TCD.a: A large, landlocked country in north-central Africa, reaching from the Sahara in the north through the Sahel to savanna in the south. Toumaï, a skull some seven million years old found in its desert, may belong to one of the oldest known members of the human family. The kingdoms of Kanem-Bornu, Baguirmi and Wadai ruled its lands before France made it a colony, and it became independent in 1960. It has more than 200 ethnic groups, and French and Arabic are its official languages. The Ennedi Plateau, with its sandstone arches and rock art, and the lakes of Ounianga in the desert are listed by UNESCO, and Zakouma National Park has brought its elephants back from the brink.
TCD.f: Lake Chad is what is left of Lake Mega-Chad, which some 7,000 years ago was about as large as the Caspian Sea.

TGO.a: A narrow strip of West Africa between Ghana and Benin, reaching more than 500 km inland from a short coast on the Gulf of Guinea. Its coast was part of the Slave Coast, from which Europeans shipped enslaved Africans across the Atlantic. Germany made it the colony of Togoland in 1884; after the First World War it was split between Britain and France, and the French part became independent as Togo in 1960, while the British part joined Ghana. Gnassingbé Eyadéma and then his son Faure Gnassingbé have led it since 1967. Lomé, its capital and port, sits right on the border with Ghana. Many of its people follow Vodun, alongside Christianity and Islam, and cocoa, coffee, cotton and phosphates are among its main exports.
TGO.f: In its Koutammakou valley the Batammariba people still build tall tower-houses of earth.

THA.a: A kingdom at the heart of mainland South-East Asia, from the mountains of the north through the rice-growing plains of the Chao Phraya to the long Malay Peninsula in the south. The kingdoms of Sukhothai and Ayutthaya, whose temple ruins are listed by UNESCO, shaped its culture, and after Ayutthaya fell in 1767 a new capital rose at Bangkok in 1782. It is the only country of South-East Asia never colonised by a European power, and was known as Siam until 1939. It has been a constitutional monarchy since 1932, and its kings are deeply revered. Most Thais are Theravada Buddhists, and tens of thousands of temples, or wats, dot the land. Its cuisine, from green curry to pad thai, is loved around the world, and the beaches and limestone islands of Phuket and Krabi make it one of the most visited countries on Earth. Muay Thai, its kickboxing, is its national sport.
THA.f: The full ceremonial name of Bangkok is the longest place name in the world.

TJK.a: A landlocked country of Central Asia, more than nine-tenths of it mountains, including much of the Pamirs, called the Roof of the World. Its people speak Tajik, a form of Persian, unlike the Turkic languages of most of their neighbours. Cities such as Panjakent belonged to Sogdiana, whose merchants traded along the Silk Road, and the Samanid dynasty of the 9th and 10th centuries is honoured as the founder of the Tajik nation. Part of the Soviet Union from the 1920s, it became independent in 1991 and suffered a civil war from 1992 to 1997. Glaciers such as the Fedchenko, one of the longest outside the polar regions, feed rivers that make it rich in hydropower, and its Nurek dam is one of the tallest in the world. The Pamir Highway, one of the highest roads on Earth, crosses its east.
TJK.f: Ismoil Somoni Peak, once called Communism Peak, was the highest mountain of the Soviet Union.

TKM.a: A country of Central Asia between the Caspian Sea and the Amu Darya river, most of it covered by the Karakum Desert. Merv, one of the great cities of the Silk Road, and the Parthian fortresses of Nisa are among its ruins, and its Turkmen people were long nomads famed for their horses and carpets. Part of the Russian Empire and then the Soviet Union, it became independent in 1991 and declared itself permanently neutral in 1995, a status recognised by the United Nations. It holds some of the world's largest reserves of natural gas, and is one of the world's most closed countries. Ashgabat, its capital, holds a world record for the number of its buildings clad in white marble. The Akhal-Teke, its golden horses, appear on its coat of arms, and the patterns of its carpets on its flag.
TKM.f: The Darvaza gas crater, the "Door to Hell", has been burning since the 1970s.

TLS.a: The eastern half of the island of Timor, with the enclave of Oecusse in the west, between Indonesia and Australia. Portugal ruled it for centuries, and it is mostly Catholic, with Tetum and Portuguese as its official languages. When Portugal left in 1975, Indonesia invaded and annexed it, and the occupation that followed cost the lives of more than 100,000 people. After a vote organised by the United Nations in 1999 chose independence, it became, in 2002, the first new sovereign state of the 21st century. Oil and gas under the Timor Sea fund most of its budget. The waters around Atauro Island have some of the richest reef life ever recorded, and it joined ASEAN in 2025.
TLS.f: It is the only country in Asia that lies entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.

TON.a: An archipelago of some 170 islands in the South Pacific, of which only a few dozen are inhabited. The Tu'i Tonga, its sacred kings, once held sway over islands across the Pacific, from Samoa to Fiji. Captain Cook called them the Friendly Islands, and Tonga is the only Pacific nation never colonised: it was a British protected state from 1900 to 1970 but kept its own king. It is the last kingdom of Polynesia, and most Tongans are devout Christians, keeping Sunday as a day of rest by law. Humpback whales come to its waters each year to breed, and visitors can swim beside them.
TON.f: The 2022 eruption of its Hunga Tonga volcano was heard as far away as Alaska.

TTO.a: Two islands at the southern end of the Caribbean, just off the coast of Venezuela: Trinidad, the larger, and Tobago. Columbus reached Trinidad in 1498, and after Spanish rule it passed to Britain, which brought enslaved Africans and later indentured workers from India to its sugar and cocoa estates. Their descendants make up most of its people, and its culture blends Africa, India, Europe and China. Independent since 1962, it is one of the richest countries in the Caribbean thanks to oil and natural gas, and the Pitch Lake, the largest natural deposit of asphalt in the world, lies on Trinidad. Its Carnival, with calypso and soca music and masquerade bands, is one of the greatest in the world. Tobago's reefs and its Main Ridge rainforest, protected since 1776, draw nature lovers.
TTO.f: The steelpan, tuned from old oil drums, was invented here in the 1930s and 1940s.

TUN.a: The northernmost country of Africa, on the Mediterranean, from the green north to the Sahara in the south. Carthage, founded by Phoenicians near today's Tunis, became a great sea power and fought three wars with Rome, which destroyed it in 146 BC. The Romans left the vast amphitheatre of El Jem, and after the Arab conquest Kairouan became one of the holiest cities of Islam. After Ottoman rule and a French protectorate it became independent in 1956. Protests that began in December 2010 toppled its president and set off the Arab Spring across the Arab world. Its old medinas, its olive groves, which make it one of the largest producers of olive oil, and the salt flats of Chott el Djerid make it a land of contrasts.
TUN.f: Luke Skywalker's desert planet, Tatooine, is named after its town of Tataouine, and parts of Star Wars were filmed here.

TUR.a: A country that bridges Europe and Asia: a small part, Eastern Thrace, lies in Europe, and the rest, the great plateau of Anatolia, in Asia, between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean. Anatolia was home to Çatalhöyük, one of the first towns, to the Hittites and to Troy, and later to Greek cities such as Ephesus. Constantinople, now Istanbul, was the capital of the Byzantine Empire for more than a thousand years, until the Ottoman Turks took it in 1453; their empire then ruled much of south-eastern Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. After the empire's defeat in the First World War, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk founded the modern Turkish republic in 1923 and made it a secular state. Istanbul, astride the Bosporus, is its largest city, and Ankara its capital. Cappadocia's fairy chimneys and cave churches, the white terraces of Pamukkale and the beaches of the Turquoise Coast draw millions of visitors. Its cuisine, from kebabs to baklava, and its tea and coffee are famous.
TUR.f: Göbekli Tepe, its rings of carved stone pillars, was raised some 11,000 years ago, long before Stonehenge.

TUV.a: A chain of nine small reef islands and atolls in the South Pacific, midway between Hawaii and Australia, the fourth-smallest country in the world. Its highest point is less than 5 m above the sea, which makes it one of the countries most threatened by rising seas. Britain ruled its Polynesian people as the Ellice Islands, together with the Gilbert Islands, now Kiribati, and it separated and became independent in 1978. In 2023 it signed a treaty with Australia that offers Tuvaluans a path to move there as the climate changes. On Funafuti, its capital atoll, the airport's runway doubles as a playing field. Fishing licences and a trust fund support its economy.
TUV.f: Its internet ending, .tv, earns it money from television and streaming sites.

TZA.a: A large country of East Africa on the Indian Ocean, including the islands of Zanzibar. Kilimanjaro, the highest mountain in Africa, rises in its north, and it borders Africa's three largest lakes, Victoria, Tanganyika and Nyasa (Malawi). Swahili traders built coastal towns such as Kilwa, and Zanzibar, ruled by the sultans of Oman, became a great market for spices and enslaved people. Tanganyika, a German and then British colony, became independent in 1961 and united with Zanzibar in 1964 to form Tanzania. Its first president, Julius Nyerere, made Swahili the language of the whole nation, helping its more than 120 peoples live together in peace. The Serengeti, where more than a million wildebeest migrate each year, and the Ngorongoro Crater are among the greatest wildlife reserves on Earth.
TZA.f: Olduvai Gorge holds some of the oldest stone tools and fossils of early humans, nearly two million years old.

UGA.a: A landlocked country of East Africa, on the equator, sitting on a high plateau around the northern shores of Lake Victoria. Winston Churchill called it the Pearl of Africa for its green beauty. The kingdom of Buganda, which gave the country its name, was one of several kingdoms that came under British rule in the 1890s, and they still have kings today as cultural leaders. Independent since 1962, it suffered under the rule of Idi Amin in the 1970s and through later wars, and the Lord's Resistance Army terrorised its north until the 2000s. The Nile flows north out of Lake Victoria at Jinja, and the Rwenzori Mountains, the Mountains of the Moon, rise on its western border with glaciers almost on the equator. Its parks are home to tree-climbing lions, chimpanzees and more than 1,000 kinds of birds.
UGA.f: Almost half of the world's mountain gorillas live in its Bwindi forest.

UKR.a: The largest country wholly in Europe, stretching from the Carpathian Mountains across wide steppes to the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov. Its black soil is among the most fertile on Earth, making it one of the world's great exporters of wheat, maize and sunflower oil, and the blue and yellow of its flag recall a sky over fields of grain. Kyiv was the heart of Kyivan Rus, a great medieval state of the East Slavs, whose Saint Sophia Cathedral still stands. Its lands were later divided between Poland-Lithuania, Russia and Austria, and the Cossacks of the steppes became a symbol of Ukrainian freedom. As part of the Soviet Union it suffered the Holodomor, the famine of 1932 and 1933 that killed millions, the devastation of the Second World War and the Chernobyl disaster of 1986. It became independent in 1991. Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, backed separatists in the east, and in 2022 launched a full-scale invasion, which Ukraine has resisted.
UKR.f: Arsenalna, in Kyiv, is the deepest metro station in the world, more than 100 m underground.

URY.a: The second-smallest country of South America, between Brazil, Argentina and the Atlantic, a land of rolling grasslands and low hills. Its gauchos herded cattle on the pampas, and beef, grilled at the asado, and mate, sipped all day from a gourd, are central to its life. Fought over by Spain and Portugal, then by Argentina and Brazil, it became independent in 1828 with British mediation. Montevideo, its capital, holds almost half of its people, and Colonia del Sacramento, an old Portuguese town across the river from Buenos Aires, is listed by UNESCO. It is one of the most stable democracies in Latin America, an early welfare state and a pioneer of social laws: in 2013 it became the first country to make the cannabis market legal. Almost all of its electricity comes from renewable sources such as wind and hydropower.
URY.f: It hosted and won the first football World Cup, in 1930.

USA.a: A federal republic of 50 states that spans North America from the Atlantic to the Pacific, with Alaska in the far north-west and Hawaii in the middle of the Pacific. Native American peoples lived across the continent for thousands of years before European settlers arrived. Thirteen British colonies on the Atlantic coast declared independence in 1776, and their constitution of 1787 is the oldest written national constitution still in use. The nation grew westward across the continent, often at the expense of Native peoples, and a civil war from 1861 to 1865 ended slavery. By 1900 it was the world's largest economy, after the Second World War it became a superpower, and in 1969 its astronauts were the first to walk on the Moon. Its people come from every part of the world, and its films, music, technology companies and universities shape life far beyond its borders. Its landscapes range from the Grand Canyon and the Rocky Mountains to the swamps of the Everglades, and New York, Los Angeles and Chicago are among the world's great cities.
USA.f: Yellowstone, created in 1872, was the first national park in the world.

UZB.a: A doubly landlocked country of Central Asia, one of only two in the world: to reach the sea you must cross two other countries. Its cities were jewels of the Silk Road: Samarkand, with its tiled Registan square, Bukhara and the walled town of Khiva. Timur, known in the West as Tamerlane, built an empire from Samarkand in the 14th century, and his grandson Ulugh Beg built one of the great observatories of the Middle Ages there. Later ruled by khanates, then by the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union, it became independent in 1991. It is the most populous country of Central Asia, and cotton, gold and natural gas are among its riches. Its bazaars, its plov, a rice dish cooked in great pots, and its blue-tiled domes are its pride.
UZB.f: The Aral Sea, on its border, has shrunk to a tenth of its size since the 1960s, when its rivers were turned to water cotton.

VAT.a: The smallest country in the world, a walled city-state of less than half a square kilometre inside Rome, ruled by the Pope as head of the Catholic Church. It became an independent state in 1929, by the Lateran Treaty with Italy, as the last remnant of the Papal States that once covered much of central Italy. Saint Peter's Basilica, by tradition built over the tomb of the apostle Peter and crowned by Michelangelo's dome, is one of the largest churches in the world. The Sistine Chapel, whose ceiling Michelangelo painted, is where the cardinals meet in conclave to elect a new pope. The Vatican Museums hold one of the world's greatest art collections, and its library and archives guard manuscripts from across the centuries. The Swiss Guard, in their striped uniforms, have protected the popes since 1506.
VAT.f: It has a cash machine with instructions in Latin.

VCT.a: Saint Vincent, a volcanic island, and the 32 islands and cays of the Grenadines, in the eastern Caribbean. The Kalinago and the Garifuna, descendants of Caribs and Africans, held Saint Vincent long after other islands were colonised, until Britain defeated them and deported most of the Garifuna to Central America in 1797. British sugar estates followed, and independence came in 1979. La Soufrière, its volcano, erupted in 1979 and again in 2021, forcing thousands to flee. The Grenadines, such as Bequia, Mustique and the Tobago Cays, are known for their sailing, beaches and reefs. Breadfruit, brought by Captain Bligh in 1793, is part of its national dish, roasted and served with fried jackfish.
VCT.f: Pirates of the Caribbean was filmed at Wallilabou Bay, on Saint Vincent.

VEN.a: A country on the Caribbean coast of South America, from the Andes in the west across the plains of the Llanos to the Orinoco and the highlands of Guayana, where flat-topped table mountains, the tepuis, rise from the forest. Columbus reached its coast in 1498, and its name, little Venice, is said to come from houses on stilts that explorers saw on Lake Maracaibo. Simón Bolívar, born in Caracas, led the wars that freed much of South America from Spain, and Venezuela became a separate republic in 1830. It holds the largest proven oil reserves in the world, which made it one of the richest countries in Latin America. Since the 2010s an economic collapse and political crisis have driven millions of Venezuelans abroad. Baseball is its favourite sport, arepas, corn cakes with fillings, are eaten every day, and lightning flickers over Lake Maracaibo on up to 260 nights a year.
VEN.f: Angel Falls, dropping from a table mountain, is the highest uninterrupted waterfall in the world.

VNM.a: A long, S-shaped country on the eastern edge of mainland South-East Asia, from the Red River delta in the north to the Mekong delta in the south. China ruled the north for about a thousand years, until Vietnam won its independence in 938, and Vietnamese dynasties later expanded south down the coast. France made it part of French Indochina in the 19th century. After the Second World War it fought France and was divided in two; the Vietnam War, between the communist north and the US-backed south, ended in 1975, and the country was reunited under communist rule. Since economic reforms began in 1986 it has become one of the fastest-growing economies in Asia, and a major exporter of electronics, clothing and coffee. Ha Long Bay, with its thousands of limestone islands, the old town of Hoi An and the imperial city of Hue are among its treasures, and pho, its noodle soup, is loved around the world.
VNM.f: Son Doong is the largest cave passage in the world, with its own jungle and clouds inside.

VUT.a: A Y-shaped chain of about 80 volcanic islands in the South Pacific, east of Australia. Melanesian peoples settled it some 3,000 years ago, and with more than 100 languages it has the most languages per person of any country. Britain and France ruled it jointly as the New Hebrides, a condominium with two of everything, from police to prisons, until independence in 1980. Bislama, a creole made mostly of English words, is spoken across the islands alongside English and French. Mount Yasur on Tanna, one of the most accessible active volcanoes in the world, has been erupting for centuries. Its sand drawings, traced in a single unbroken line, are listed by UNESCO.
VUT.f: The land divers of Pentecost Island, who leap from tall towers tied by vines, inspired bungee jumping.

WSM.a: Two large volcanic islands, Upolu and Savai'i, with a few smaller ones, in the heart of Polynesia in the South Pacific. Polynesians have lived here for some 3,000 years, and fa'a Samoa, the Samoan way, built on extended families led by chiefs called matai, still shapes daily life. Germany ruled it from 1900 and New Zealand from 1914, and in 1962 it became the first Pacific island nation of the 20th century to gain independence. The writer Robert Louis Stevenson spent his last years here, and is buried on Mount Vaea above Apia. Rugby is a passion, and the pe'a, the traditional tattoo of Samoan men, covers the body from the waist to the knees.
WSM.f: In 2011 it skipped 30 December, moving west of the date line to share its days with Australia and New Zealand.

YEM.a: A country at the south-western corner of the Arabian Peninsula, on the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, with mountains rising to cool, green highlands. Ancient kingdoms such as Saba, the biblical Sheba, grew rich here on the trade in frankincense and myrrh, and the great dam of Marib was one of the engineering marvels of the ancient world. The old city of Sana'a, with its tall brick houses decorated with white patterns, has been lived in for more than 2,500 years. Coffee was first traded from its port of Mocha, which gave its name to a kind of coffee. North and South Yemen united in 1990. A civil war that began in 2014 has caused one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world. Socotra, its island in the Arabian Sea, has dragon's blood trees and plants found nowhere else.
YEM.f: Shibam, a walled town of mud-brick tower houses, is called the Manhattan of the desert.

ZAF.a: The southernmost country of Africa, where the Atlantic and Indian Oceans meet, from the deserts of the west to the high Drakensberg mountains and the subtropical east. Fossils from the Cradle of Humankind, near Johannesburg, are among the oldest of human ancestors, and its San people left rock paintings thousands of years old. The Dutch East India Company founded Cape Town in 1652, and Britain later took the Cape; gold and diamonds, found in the 19th century, made it the most industrialised country of Africa. From 1948 its white minority government enforced apartheid, a system of racial segregation, until it was dismantled after years of struggle. Nelson Mandela, freed after 27 years in prison, became its first democratically elected president in 1994. It has twelve official languages, including sign language, and calls itself the rainbow nation. Table Mountain, the Cape of Good Hope and Kruger National Park, home to the big five, draw visitors from around the world.
ZAF.f: It has three capitals: Pretoria for the government, Cape Town for parliament and Bloemfontein for the courts.

ZMB.a: A landlocked country on a high plateau in southern Africa, named after the Zambezi river, which forms much of its southern border. Victoria Falls, called Mosi-oa-Tunya, the smoke that thunders, lies on its border with Zimbabwe. Once the British colony of Northern Rhodesia, it became independent in 1964 under Kenneth Kaunda, and has been one of Africa's more peaceful countries, with democratic changes of government. Copper, mined in the Copperbelt, has long been the backbone of its economy. South Luangwa, home to leopards and the birthplace of walking safaris, and Kafue are among its great national parks, and every year some ten million straw-coloured fruit bats gather at Kasanka, one of the largest mammal migrations on Earth. It has more than 70 ethnic groups, and English is its official language.
ZMB.f: Lake Kariba, on its border with Zimbabwe, is the largest reservoir in the world by volume.

ZWE.a: A landlocked country of southern Africa between the Zambezi and the Limpopo rivers, mostly a high plateau. Great Zimbabwe, a stone city built between the 11th and 15th centuries, was the capital of a trading kingdom and gave the country its name, which means houses of stone. It was the British colony of Southern Rhodesia; its white minority government declared independence in 1965, and after a long war of liberation it became independent as Zimbabwe in 1980. Robert Mugabe led it from then until 2017, years that saw a fast-track land reform and, in 2008, one of the worst bouts of hyperinflation ever recorded. Its national parks, such as Hwange and Mana Pools, are home to great herds of elephants. The soapstone Zimbabwe Bird, found at Great Zimbabwe, appears on its flag.
ZWE.f: Victoria Falls, on its border with Zambia, is the largest curtain of falling water in the world.
